### 2026-08-05

Completed

- Payment Receive (eleventh Accounting module — records a customer payment and allocates it against one or more open Sales Invoices, updating each invoice's `amount_paid`/`invoice_status` as a side effect)

Scope decision

- Inspected `SalesInvoice` (its `balance_due` accessor, `STATUSES` enum), `SalesInvoiceService`/`Controller`/`Request`, `FinanceBankAccount`, and the two established "record a payment" precedents already in this codebase (`SalesCommissionService::markAsPaid()`/`PayrollService::markAsPaid()` — binary mark-paid, no partial concept; `EmployeeLoanService::recordPayment()` — closer analog, increments `paid_amount` directly on the loan record, no separate history table) directly before starting. Neither existing precedent writes to a separate ledger/transaction table, but a real "Payment Receive" needs its own record (date, method, bank account, reference) and — since a single payment can reasonably cover multiple invoices in one receipt — this is genuinely new master-detail territory for this project: a header (the payment itself) + items (per-invoice allocations), not a single-table "mark as paid" toggle.
- **New reference-number prefix `PMT-`** — confirmed `PR-` was already taken by Purchase Requests before picking this, checked against every other prefix used in this project (`SQ-`/`SO-`/`DLV-`/`DN-`/`INV-`/`CN-`/`RET-`/`POS-`/`RFQ-`/`SUPQ-`/`PO-`/`GRN-`/`PINV-`/`DBN-`/`PRET-`/`SE-`/`OS-`/`ADJ-`/`ST-`/`SC-`/`JE-`/CRM's `QUO-`) to avoid any collision.
- **`payment_receive_allocations` has no unique constraint on `(payment_receive_id, sales_invoice_id)`** — unlike most junction-style item tables in this project, a genuinely repeated allocation to the same invoice within one payment isn't a meaningful use case here (unlike, say, a product appearing twice on a sales order at different discounts), but nothing about the schema forbids it either; the Form Request's `distinct` rule on `items.*.sales_invoice_id` is the actual guard against accidental duplicate rows, same "app-level guard, not a DB constraint, for a UX safeguard rather than a hard business rule" reasoning used elsewhere (e.g. Purchase Orders' non-unique product lines).
- **New service pattern for this project, building on Bank Reconciliation's precedent**: `PaymentReceiveService` doesn't just delete-then-recreate allocation rows — `update()`/`delete()` first *reverse* every previously-applied allocation (subtracting it back out of the linked invoice's `amount_paid` and re-deriving `invoice_status`) before removing the old rows and re-applying the new set. This is the same "unmark before delete-then-recreate" sequence `BankReconciliationService` established for `BankTransaction.reconciled`, generalized here from a boolean flag to a running numeric total plus a derived status enum.
- **`deriveInvoiceStatus()` never touches a `cancelled` invoice** — a cancelled invoice was never actually billed, so no amount of payment activity against it (including a reversal) should resurrect its status; every other invoice's status is freshly derived from its own `grand_total`/`amount_paid` after each apply/reverse (`paid` when balance ≤ 0, `partially_paid` when something's been paid but not enough, `sent` as the fallback when a reversal brings `amount_paid` back to exactly 0) — verified directly in testing across a full apply → partial-reverse → full-reverse cycle.
- **New cross-field validation in the Form Request, beyond the usual uniqueness/cycle checks**: `PaymentReceiveRequest::withValidator()` rejects an allocation against an invoice that doesn't belong to the header's selected customer (preventing a payment from silently misapplying to someone else's invoice), and rejects an allocation amount exceeding the invoice's currently *available* balance — computed as `balance_due + (this same payment's own prior allocation to that invoice, if editing)`, so re-submitting an unchanged allocation on an edit is never incorrectly flagged as "exceeds balance" just because the reversal hasn't happened yet at validation time.
- **New client-side interaction pattern**: the item-row invoice `<option>` list is preloaded once (every open, non-cancelled invoice with `amount_paid < grand_total`, each carrying `data-customer-id`/`data-balance`) and JS filters which options are visible per row based on the header's currently-selected customer — changing the customer clears any row selection that no longer belongs to it. This is a new "cross-field filtering" technique for this project's item-row JS (every prior repeatable-row builder filtered nothing beyond what was preloaded), needed here because, unlike a product catalog (the same for every document), which invoices are valid depends on which customer is selected.
- **A route-parameter mis-pluralization bug was caught and fixed during verification**: `Route::resource('payment-receives', ...)` initially generated the URI wildcard `{payment_receife}` — Doctrine's Inflector singularizes `-ives` endings the same way it does `wives → wife`/`knives → knife`, which doesn't apply to "receives". Since implicit route-model-binding matches the URI wildcard name (snake_cased) against the controller method's parameter name, `$paymentReceive` (→ `payment_receive`) would never have matched `payment_receife`, silently breaking edit/update/destroy. Fixed with an explicit `->parameters(['payment-receives' => 'payment_receive'])` override — confirmed via `route:list` that all three model-bound routes now correctly show `{payment_receive}`.

Database

- Added `payment_receives`/`payment_receive_allocations` in one migration (`database/migrations/2026_08_05_090000_create_payment_receives_table.php`):
  - `payment_receives`: `payment_number` unique (server-generated); `customer_id` required `foreignId` → `customers.id`, `cascadeOnDelete` (same reasoning as every required parent-owns-child FK in this project); `finance_bank_account_id` nullable `foreignId` → `finance_bank_accounts.id`, `nullOnDelete` (a cash payment has no bank account at all); `payment_date` required date; `payment_method` enum (`cash`/`bank_transfer`/`cheque`/`card`/`other`) default `cash`; `reference` nullable string; `amount` decimal(15,2) default 0, server-computed only (sum of allocations, never client-submitted, same convention as every other server-computed total in this project); `notes` nullable text; `status` boolean.
  - `payment_receive_allocations`: `payment_receive_id`/`sales_invoice_id` both `cascadeOnDelete`; `amount_allocated` decimal(15,2) default 0. No unique constraint, per the Scope decision above.

Models

- Added `App\Models\PaymentReceive` — fillable `payment_number, customer_id, finance_bank_account_id, payment_date, payment_method, reference, amount, notes, status`; `public const METHODS = ['cash','bank_transfer','cheque','card','other']`; casts `status` boolean, `payment_date` to `date`, `amount` to `decimal:2`; relations `customer()`, `financeBankAccount()`, `items(): HasMany` (→ `PaymentReceiveAllocation`); `scopeActive()`.
- Added `App\Models\PaymentReceiveAllocation` — fillable `payment_receive_id, sales_invoice_id, amount_allocated`; casts `amount_allocated` to `decimal:2`; relations `paymentReceive()`, `salesInvoice()`.

Services

- Added `App\Services\PaymentReceiveService` — `generatePaymentNumber()` (`'PMT-' . str_pad(PaymentReceive::max('id')+1, 6, '0', STR_PAD_LEFT)`); `create()` computes `amount` from submitted items then applies each allocation onto its invoice; `update()` reverses every existing allocation first, deletes the old rows, recomputes `amount`, updates the header, then re-applies the new set; `delete()` reverses every allocation then deletes the header (allocation rows cascade via FK). `applyItems()`/`reverseItems()`/`deriveInvoiceStatus()` are the new cross-table logic described in the Scope decision above.

Requests

- Added `App\Http\Requests\Admin\PaymentReceiveRequest` — `customer_id` required `exists:customers,id`; `finance_bank_account_id` nullable `exists:finance_bank_accounts,id`; `payment_date` required date; `payment_method` required `Rule::in(PaymentReceive::METHODS)`; `reference`/`notes`/`status` standard; `items` required array `min:1` with `items.*.sales_invoice_id` required `distinct` `exists:sales_invoices,id` and `items.*.amount_allocated` required numeric `min:0.01`. The `withValidator()` closure (customer-ownership check + available-balance check, described above) is the module's core new logic.

Controllers

- Added `App\Http\Controllers\Admin\PaymentReceiveController` — index eager-loads `customer`/`financeBankAccount` and `withCount('items')`; adds `customer_id`/`payment_method` AJAX filters; search matches `payment_number` or the customer's `name`. DataTable's `payment_number` column subtitles the customer name; `payment_method_badge` is a plain secondary badge (no color-per-method map, since none of the 5 methods carries more "success/danger" meaning than another). `create()`/`edit()` load active `Customer`s/`FinanceBankAccount`s and a shared `openInvoices()` helper — active, non-cancelled invoices with `amount_paid < grand_total` (the SQL-comparable equivalent of `balance_due > 0`, since `balance_due` is an accessor, not a column), plus (on edit) this Payment Receive's own already-allocated invoices via `orWhereIn`, so editing never loses the currently-selected invoice from the dropdown even if it's now fully paid. `store()`/`update()`/`destroy()` all `load('items')` before logging to `ActivityLogger`, same technique as every prior master-detail module.

Views

- Added `resources/views/admin/payment-receives/{index,create,edit,action}.blade.php` — `'modal' => 'lg'` (invoice + amount = 2-field item rows, same width justification as Delivery Management's/Purchase Requests' simpler item rows, not the wider `'xl'` used by 4-field pricing documents). `index.blade.php` adds "All Customers" and "All Payment Methods" filter dropdowns. `create.blade.php`/`edit.blade.php`: header fields (Customer, Bank Account, Payment Date, Payment Method, Reference, Status, Notes) plus the repeatable `.payment-receive-item-rows` builder and a live "Total Allocated" preview (summed client-side, purely a UX convenience — the authoritative `amount` is always computed server-side from the submitted items).

JS

- Added `public/assets/system/js/pages/payment-receives.js` — `buildPaymentReceiveItemRow()`/`populateExistingPaymentReceiveItems()`/`observeModalContent()` trio adapted from the project's standard 2-field item-row pattern (e.g. `deliveries.js`), plus two genuinely new pieces: an amount-auto-fill-from-the-selected-invoice's-`data-balance` behavior (same "auto-fill, never overwrite an already-typed value" convention used by every pricing-document item row), and `filterPaymentReceiveInvoiceOptions()` — the new cross-field filtering described in the Scope decision above, bound to the header customer select's `change` event and re-run on every new row's creation.

Routes

The explicit `->parameters()` override fixes the mis-pluralization bug described above.

Scope decision

- Inspected `GeneralLedgerController` and its Blade view directly before starting. Same "controller only, no new table/Model/Service/Request" shape already used by General Ledger, Cash Book, Accounts Receivable, and Accounts Payable — a single `GET` route, one controller `index()`, one Blade view.
- Per this project's established precedent (documented explicitly in Stock Valuation's, Low Stock Alerts', and General Ledger's own changelog entries), **no shared service was extracted** with `GeneralLedgerController` despite the overlapping aggregation — each report controller computes its own aggregation independently, so editing one report later can never accidentally change another's behavior.
- **Uses raw `debit - credit` per account, NOT General Ledger's `normal_balance`-aware signed sum** — a deliberate, documented divergence from the report it extends. A trial balance's entire purpose is to show the *natural ledger side* each account actually sits on (positive net → Debit column, negative net → Credit column), so that the two columns sum to the same figure. General Ledger's signed sum deliberately flips the sign for credit-normal accounts so a revenue account's balance reads as a positive "how much revenue" figure — correct for a per-account running balance, but it would make a trial balance's two columns fail to reconcile. `normal_balance` is still carried through and displayed per row, so an account sitting on the opposite side of its expected normal balance is visible to the reader rather than silently normalized away.
- **Only `entry_status = 'posted'` journal entries are counted** — the same stricter-than-Inventory filter General Ledger/Cash Book established (a `draft` entry isn't yet a financial fact; a `cancelled` one never happened). Verified directly in testing: a draft entry's amounts were correctly excluded from the totals.
- **Only postable (non-group) `ChartOfAccount`s appear** — a group/header account can never receive a journal line (enforced since Journal Entries), so including it would add nothing but empty rows. Verified in testing that a group account was correctly excluded.
- **Balance check is surfaced, not hidden**: `difference = totalDebit - totalCredit` is shown as its own stat tile alongside a green "Balanced" / red "Out of Balance" badge, with the footer totals turning red when out of balance. In a correctly-functioning system this can never be non-zero (Journal Entries' own Form Request already rejects an unbalanced entry), so a non-zero value here is a genuine data-integrity signal worth making loud rather than a routine state — the first report in this project whose headline figure is a self-diagnostic rather than a business metric.
- Three filters, all plain `GET` form fields submitting on `change` (the standard read-only-report filter pattern in this project): `as_of_date` (a single cut-off date, not a range — a trial balance is a point-in-time snapshot, unlike General Ledger's from/to range), `account_type` (the 5 fixed natures, sourced from `ChartOfAccount::ACCOUNT_TYPES`), and `hide_zero` (drop accounts with no net balance — useful once a chart of accounts grows past a screenful of mostly-dormant accounts).

### 2026-08-09 (2)

Scope decision

- Inspected `TrialBalanceController`/`GeneralLedgerController` and their views directly before starting. Same "controller only, no new table/Model/Service/Request" shape already used by General Ledger, Cash Book, Accounts Receivable, Accounts Payable, and Trial Balance — a single `GET` route, one controller `index()`, one Blade view. Per this project's established precedent (documented in Stock Valuation's, Low Stock Alerts', General Ledger's and Trial Balance's own changelog entries), **no shared service was extracted** — each report controller computes its own aggregation independently.
- **A period report, not a point-in-time snapshot** — the key structural difference from Trial Balance, which was built the same day. Trial Balance takes a single `as_of_date` cut-off across *every* account; a P&L takes a `date_from`/`date_to` **range** (the General Ledger filter shape) and reads only the two **nominal** account types, `revenue` and `expense`. Asset/liability/equity accounts are balance-sheet accounts and are deliberately excluded here — they belong to the Balance Sheet report (the next roadmap item). Verified in testing that an `asset` account with real posted activity in the period correctly never appears in either section.
- **Direction is fixed per account type, not read from the account's `normal_balance` accessor** — revenue is earned on the credit side (`credit - debit`), expense is incurred on the debit side (`debit - credit`), so both sections report a positive-is-normal `amount` and the statement reads naturally as "revenue less expenses." This is a third distinct treatment of the same underlying journal lines across the three report modules built so far: General Ledger uses the `normal_balance`-aware signed sum (so a running balance reads positively for its own account type), Trial Balance uses raw `debit - credit` (so the two columns reconcile), and Profit and Loss uses a per-section fixed direction (so both sections read as positive magnitudes). Each is correct for its own report's purpose; documented explicitly here since the three look superficially similar.
- **A negative line amount is reported as-is, not clamped to zero** — a refund or reversal can legitimately push a revenue or expense line negative (revenue net of refunds), which is real information rather than an error to hide; such lines render in red so they stand out without being suppressed.
- **`profitMargin` is `null`, not `0`, when there is no revenue** — a margin has no meaning with a zero denominator, so the tile shows `-` rather than a misleading `0.00%`, the same "meaningful label instead of a bare zero" idiom used by Stock Valuation's "No cost data" and Low Stock Alerts' dash-instead-of-zero columns.
- **Only `entry_status = 'posted'` journal entries are counted** — the same stricter-than-Inventory filter every prior Accounting report uses. Verified in testing: a draft entry's 999 expense was correctly excluded, as was a posted revenue entry dated outside the selected range.
- Each account name links through to that account's own General Ledger detail view, carrying `date_from`/`date_to` forward — the same drill-down navigation Trial Balance and General Ledger's summary already established.

### 2026-08-09 (3)

Completed

- Balance Sheet (fifteenth Accounting module — the financial position as of a date: total assets on one side, total liabilities plus equity on the other, with a built-in balance check)

Scope decision

- Inspected `ProfitAndLossController`/`TrialBalanceController`/`GeneralLedgerController` and their views directly before starting. Same "controller only, no new table/Model/Service/Request" shape as every prior Accounting report. Per this project's established precedent (documented in Stock Valuation's, Low Stock Alerts', General Ledger's, Trial Balance's and Profit and Loss's own changelog entries), **no shared service was extracted** — each report controller computes its own aggregation independently.
- **The complement of Profit and Loss**: P&L covers the two **nominal** types (`revenue`/`expense`) over a *period*; the Balance Sheet covers the three **real** types (`asset`/`liability`/`equity`) as of a single *cut-off date*. Together the two reports account for all five `ChartOfAccount::ACCOUNT_TYPES`. Filter shape follows Trial Balance's (`as_of_date`, a point-in-time snapshot) rather than P&L's date range.
- **Retained earnings is computed at report time, not read from a posted closing entry** — the module's single most important design decision. No module in this project ever closes nominal accounts out into a real equity account (there is no year-end closing routine, and Journal Entries has no such automation), so without adding cumulative revenue-less-expenses into equity the two sides of the sheet would never reconcile. `calculateRetainedEarnings()` therefore sums all posted revenue less all posted expenses up to the same cut-off date and presents it as a distinct "Retained Earnings" equity line, explicitly labelled in the view as computed rather than a posted account so no one goes looking for it in the Chart of Accounts. Verified directly in testing: a capital injection + loan + revenue + expense scenario reconciled to the cent only because retained earnings was included.
- **`active()` scoping is applied identically in `buildRows()` and `calculateRetainedEarnings()`** — a deliberate, commented consistency guard: if one method filtered inactive accounts and the other didn't, an inactive nominal account with a balance would silently unbalance the sheet. Both use `active()`, matching Trial Balance's own scoping.
- **Direction is fixed per section, not read from `normal_balance`** — assets on the debit side (`debit - credit`), liabilities and equity on the credit side (`credit - debit`) — the same per-section fixed-direction approach Profit and Loss uses, so every section reads as a positive magnitude. This is now the third distinct treatment of the same journal lines across the report modules (General Ledger's `normal_balance`-aware signed sum, Trial Balance's raw `debit - credit`, and this per-section fixed direction), each correct for its own report's purpose.
- **A negative line is reported as-is, not clamped** — e.g. an overdrawn bank account sitting on the credit side renders in red rather than being suppressed, same convention as Profit and Loss's negative revenue lines.
- **Out-of-balance is surfaced loudly**: alongside the green "Balanced" / red "Out of Balance" stat badge, a dedicated red callout card appears below the statement naming the exact difference and both totals, and pointing the reader at the Trial Balance to find the offending postings. In a correctly-functioning system this can never fire (Journal Entries rejects unbalanced entries), so its appearance is a genuine data-integrity signal — the same "self-diagnostic headline" reasoning Trial Balance's own difference tile established, taken one step further with an actionable message.
- **Only `entry_status = 'posted'` journal entries are counted** — the same stricter-than-Inventory filter every prior Accounting report uses. Verified in testing: a draft entry and a posted entry dated after the cut-off were both correctly excluded.
- Each account name links through to its own General Ledger detail view carrying `date_to` forward — the same drill-down navigation Trial Balance and Profit and Loss already established.

Database

- **No new tables** — reads `journal_entry_items`/`journal_entries` and `chart_of_accounts`, all already built. No Model, no Service, no Form Request, no CRUD routes. Confirmed `php artisan migrate` was not needed.

### 2026-08-09 (4)

Completed

- Cash Flow (sixteenth Accounting module — a direct-method statement of every cash movement over a period, classified into Operating, Investing and Financing activities, reconciling opening cash to closing cash)

Scope decision

- Inspected `CashBookController` (for its established cash-account heuristic) and `BalanceSheetController`/`ProfitAndLossController` (for report structure) directly before starting. Same "controller only, no new table/Model/Service/Request" shape as every prior Accounting report. Per this project's established precedent (documented in Stock Valuation's, Low Stock Alerts', General Ledger's, Trial Balance's, Profit and Loss's and Balance Sheet's own changelog entries), **no shared service was extracted** — each report controller computes its own aggregation independently.
- **Direct method, deliberately not indirect** — the module's defining decision. An indirect-method statement starts from net profit and adjusts for non-cash items and working-capital movements, which requires distinguishing current from non-current balance-sheet accounts; `chart_of_accounts` has no such flag and inventing one would be a schema change well outside this module's scope. The direct method reads actual cash movements straight from the journal, which this data model supports exactly — both the more accurate and the more honest choice given the available data.
- **Classification is derived from the contra account on the same journal entry**, not from any new column: for each posted entry that touches cash, the non-cash lines determine where the money came from or went — `revenue`/`expense` → Operating, other `asset` → Investing, `liability`/`equity` → Financing. This is genuinely new logic for this project: every prior Accounting report aggregated lines account-by-account in isolation, whereas this one must read each journal entry **as a whole** to see what the cash was exchanged for.
- **Compound entries are split proportionally**: when one entry's cash movement faces several contra accounts, the net cash figure is allocated across them in proportion to each contra line's own magnitude, so a single entry can legitimately contribute to more than one activity. Pure cash-to-cash transfers (an entry whose only lines are cash accounts) net to zero and are skipped entirely rather than appearing as two offsetting rows.
- **Movements are grouped per contra account**, not listed per journal line — the statement reads as a short list of named sources and uses of cash, which is what a cash flow statement is for; per-line detail remains one click away via the existing General Ledger drill-down link on each row.
- **Built-in reconciliation check**: the closing figure derived by summing classified flows is cross-checked against the cash accounts' own raw balance at the cut-off date, computed independently. Any mismatch (which would mean a cash movement escaped classification) surfaces as a red callout naming the difference, both figures, and the unattributed amount — the same "self-diagnostic surfaced, not hidden" approach Trial Balance's difference tile and Balance Sheet's out-of-balance callout established. An `unclassified` bucket captures the pathological case of cash moving with no non-cash counterpart at all, so such an entry shows up in the difference rather than being silently absorbed.
- **Reuses Cash Book's cash-account heuristic verbatim** (a postable, `asset`-natured account whose assigned Account Type is named something containing "cash" or "bank"), including the same honest empty state — a message with direct links to Account Types and Chart of Accounts — when no such account has been configured, rather than guessing at which accounts are cash-like. Same known-limitation caveat Cash Book already documents.
- **Only `entry_status = 'posted'` journal entries are read** — the same stricter-than-Inventory filter every prior Accounting report uses. Verified in testing: a draft entry was correctly excluded, and a posted entry dated before the period correctly contributed to the opening balance rather than to any activity section.

Database

- **No new tables** — reads `journal_entries`/`journal_entry_items`, `chart_of_accounts` and `account_types` (via the `ChartOfAccount::accountType()` relation), all already built. No Model, no Service, no Form Request, no CRUD routes. Confirmed `php artisan migrate` was not needed.

Models

- No new or modified models. `JournalEntry::items()` and `JournalEntryItem::chartOfAccount()` (both pre-existing) are eager-loaded together as `items.chartOfAccount` — the first place in this project's Accounting reports that loads the journal from the entry side rather than the item side, since classification needs each entry's full line set at once.

Services

- No service — read-only report, per the established report-controller pattern.

Requests

- No Form Request — all inputs are optional `GET` filters read directly off the `Request`.

Controllers

- Added `App\Http\Controllers\Admin\CashFlowController` — `index()` resolves the cash-account set, computes `openingBalance` via `cashBalanceBefore()`, classifies the period's movements via `buildFlows()`, splits the result into the three activity sections, then derives `netChange`/`closingBalance` and cross-checks against `cashBalanceAsOf()` to produce `reconciliationDifference`/`isReconciled`. `classify()` maps a contra account type onto its activity via a `match` expression.

Views

- Added `resources/views/admin/cash-flow/index.blade.php` — a full-page (non-modal) report view with 4 `.stat-card` tiles (the three activity totals plus Closing Cash, each red when negative) and three stacked `.nx-card` section tables rendered from a single `@foreach` over a `@php`-defined `$sections` array — a new loop-driven section pattern for this project's reports, chosen over three copy-pasted card blocks since the three sections are structurally identical. A final reconciliation card lays the statement out in conventional form (opening cash, the three net figures, net change, closing cash) with the red mismatch callout rendered via `@unless($isReconciled)`. The empty-state branch (no cash accounts configured) mirrors Cash Book's own.

JS

- None — filters are plain `onchange="this.form.submit()"` form controls, same as every other read-only report page in this project. No DataTable, no chart.

Routes

Inserted live via `Permission::firstOrCreate(['name' => ..., 'guard_name' => 'admin'])` and synced onto "Super Admin" via tinker per established precedent (seeder still not idempotent, not re-run wholesale).

### 2026-08-09 (5)

Completed

- Tax Management (seventeenth Accounting module — a master of configurable tax rates, each optionally linked to the ledger accounts its output and input tax post to)

Scope decision

- Checked the Naming/Table Conflict Guard and every existing migration first: **no `tax_rates`/`taxes` table existed anywhere**, and the only pre-existing tax-related columns in the codebase are the free-text `tax_number` fields on `customers`/`vendors` (a party's registration number, an entirely different concept). No collision.
- **A full CRUD master, not a report** — the first non-report Accounting module since Payment Make, and the first CRUD module in the whole Accounting sequence to sit under the "Accounting Masters" group rather than getting a top-level link. Follows the flat `FinanceBankAccount` shape exactly (Controller → Service → Model, Form Request, `ActivityLogger`, Yajra DataTables + `ajax-form` modal), not the header+items master-detail shape.
- **Two separate GL account links (`sales_account_id` / `purchase_account_id`), not one** — output tax collected on sales is a liability owed to the tax authority, while input tax paid on purchases is typically a recoverable asset; they post to genuinely different accounts, so collapsing them into a single `chart_of_account_id` (the way `FinanceBankAccount` has one) would have forced a business to choose one side or create two near-duplicate tax records. Both are nullable/`nullOnDelete` — a tax rate remains a valid record if a linked account is later deleted, verified in testing (`sales_account_id` correctly went to `NULL`, the rate survived).
- **Reuses the "no posting to group accounts" rule Journal Entries and Bank Accounts already enforce** — `TaxRateRequest::withValidator()` rejects either account field pointing at a group/header account, with the error naming which of the two fields is at fault; the controller additionally excludes group accounts from both dropdowns entirely (defense in depth, the same pattern used throughout this project).
- **`rate` is `decimal(8,4)`, not `decimal(5,2)`** — real-world rates are not always whole or two-decimal (e.g. 7.5%, 12.375% in some jurisdictions), and a 4-decimal scale costs nothing. Validated `0`–`100` at the Form Request level with a dedicated message, the same "a percentage logically can't exceed 100" rule `DiscountRuleRequest` already established for percentage discounts.
- **`is_current` is a computed accessor, not a stored flag** — whether a rate is in force today follows entirely from `effective_from`/`effective_to` (both optional; a rate with neither is always current). Storing it would require a scheduled job to keep it truthful as dates pass, so it is derived on read, the same reasoning behind `SalesInvoice::balance_due`, `StockCountItem::variance` and Balance Sheet's computed retained earnings. Surfaced in the DataTable as a green "Current" / grey "Not in force" badge beneath the date range — verified in testing that a rate whose window closed in 2021 correctly reports `false`.
- **`tax_type` (`exclusive`/`inclusive`), `applies_to` (`sales`/`purchase`/`both`) and `is_compound` are captured but not yet consumed by any transaction module** — Sales/Purchase documents have no tax fields today, so this module defines the master data those modules would read once tax-on-documents is requested. Deliberately **no retrofit of tax columns onto `sales_invoices`/`purchase_invoices` was attempted** — that is a change to two already-shipped modules well beyond this checklist item, and would need its own request. Flagged here explicitly so a future task knows the master exists and is unconsumed.

Custom `messages()` for the unique, max-100 and date-ordering rules, plus the `withValidator()` group-account closure described above.

Index eager-loads both account relations, adds an `applies_to` AJAX filter beyond the standard `status`/`search`, search matches `name` or `code`. DataTable columns: `name` (with the code as a subtitle and a "Compound" badge when set), `rate_formatted` (trailing zeros stripped so `15.0000` reads as `15%`, the same `rtrim(rtrim(...))` technique `UnitConversionController` established), `tax_type_label`, `applies_to_badge` (own 3-colour map), `validity` (formatted date range or "Always", plus the computed Current / Not-in-force badge), `status_badge`. ### 2026-08-09 (6)

Completed — **Accounting module is now fully complete (18/18 roadmap features)**

- Financial Reports (eighteenth and final Accounting module — the module's landing dashboard: every statement's headline figures on one screen, a month-by-month revenue/expense trend, and a directory linking through to each full statement)

Scope decision

- Same "controller only, no new table/Model/Service/Request" shape as every other Accounting report, and the same closing-module role `SalesReportController`/`PurchaseReportController`/`InventoryReportController` play for their own sections.
- **Recomputes every figure independently rather than calling into the individual statement controllers.** Per this project's established precedent (documented in Stock Valuation's, Low Stock Alerts', General Ledger's, Trial Balance's, Profit and Loss's, Balance Sheet's and Cash Flow's own changelog entries), each report owns its aggregation — so a future change to, say, Profit and Loss can never silently change what this dashboard reports, and vice versa. That means the per-type direction rules (nominal accounts positive-is-normal, real accounts by side) and the report-time retained-earnings computation are deliberately repeated here rather than shared.
- **A trend, not another statement** — the monthly revenue/expense/net series is the one figure no individual statement provides, since each of them reports a single period or a single point in time. It defaults to the last 6 months when no date range is given so the chart is never empty on first load, is derived from the selected range otherwise, and is hard-capped at 24 iterations with an inverted-range guard so a nonsensical filter can never produce a runaway loop.
- **Draft entries are called out rather than silently dropped.** Like every prior Accounting report, only `entry_status = 'posted'` entries feed the figures — but this dashboard additionally counts outstanding drafts and, when any exist, prints a red note in the statement-directory header stating exactly how many are excluded from every number above. Verified in testing: a draft entry's 900 was excluded from revenue while the draft count correctly reported 1.
- **Receivables/payables read the invoice tables directly** (not the ledger), matching how Accounts Receivable/Payable themselves work. `balance_due` is an accessor rather than a column on both invoice models, so the sums are computed in PHP — the same constraint those two reports and Sales/Purchase Reports already work around identically. Outstanding totals are floored at zero per invoice so an overpaid invoice cannot net against genuinely owed balances.
- **A balance check is surfaced here too** — the Balance Sheet's assets-vs-liabilities-plus-equity reconciliation is repeated as a badge on this page, so the dashboard reports whether the books balance rather than presenting figures that might not.
- The statement directory carries the current `date_from`/`date_to` through to each linked report, so a range selected here follows the user into whichever statement they open.

Database

- **No new tables** — reads `journal_entries`/`journal_entry_items`, `chart_of_accounts`, `account_types`, `sales_invoices`, `purchase_invoices` and `tax_rates`, all already built. No Model, no Service, no Form Request, no CRUD routes. Confirmed `php artisan migrate` was not needed.

Models

- No new or modified models.

Services

- No service — read-only report, per the established report-controller pattern.

Requests

- No Form Request — the two date filters are optional `GET` parameters read directly off the `Request`.

Controllers

- Added `App\Http\Controllers\Admin\FinancialReportController` — `index()` assembles the P&L headline (`nominalTotal()` for revenue/expense, plus net profit and margin), the Balance Sheet headline (`realTotal()` per real type plus report-time `retainedEarnings` and a balance check), the cash position (`cashBalance()`, reusing Cash Book's cash-account heuristic verbatim including its zero-when-unconfigured behaviour), receivables/payables via a shared `outstanding()` helper parameterised by model class, ledger-health counts (posted entries in period, outstanding drafts, active tax rates), and the `monthlyTrend()` series. `itemsForType()` is the single shared query builder every account-type aggregation goes through, so the posted-only and active/non-group filters can never drift between sections of this one page.

Views

### 2026-08-09 (7)

Completed

- Asset Categories (first Asset Management module — the foundational classification master, same starting-point role Chart of Accounts played for Accounting, Warehouses for Inventory, Vendors for Purchase and Customers for Sales)

Scope decision

- Checked the Naming/Table Conflict Guard and every existing migration first: **no `asset_categories` table, `AssetCategory` model, or any asset-related table existed anywhere**. The Product Management module owns a `categories` table, but that is product classification with its own self-referencing tree — an entirely separate concern from asset classification, and the two names do not collide.
- **Flat lookup, deliberately not a self-referencing tree** — unlike Product Management's `categories` (which was retrofitted into a `parent_id` tree at explicit client request to absorb the "Sub Categories" roadmap item), erp.txt's Asset Management checklist lists no "Asset Sub Categories" feature, so asset categories stay a single-level master in the shape of `Brand`/`Unit`/`PriceTier`. If nesting is ever requested, the same `parent_id` retrofit Categories already went through is available.
- **Depreciation defaults are captured now, ahead of the module that will consume them** — `depreciation_method` (`none`/`straight_line`/`reducing_balance`), `useful_life_years` and `salvage_value_percent` live on the category rather than being deferred to the "Depreciation Calculation" roadmap item. This is the same "define the master the later module will read" reasoning that put `is_group` on Chart of Accounts ahead of Journal Entries enforcing it, and `reconciled`/`reconciled_date` on Bank Transactions ahead of Bank Reconciliation using them. Asset Register (the next module) will presumably inherit these as per-asset defaults, and Depreciation Calculation will read the method to decide how to spread cost — neither is implemented here.
- **`useful_life_years` is conditionally required, not blanket-required** — `required_unless:depreciation_method,none`, since a non-depreciating category (land, for example) has no life to spread cost over. The create/edit forms hide the field entirely when "None" is selected, mirroring the validation rule in the UI rather than leaving a required-looking field that can never apply — the same `MutationObserver`-driven conditional-field technique `discount-rules.js`/`customers.js` already established for this project's remote modals. Verified both branches in testing.
- **Both `name` and `code` are unique** — a code is the compact identifier an asset tag or register line will reference, so it must be unambiguous; unlike `Warehouse.code` (also user-entered) there is no auto-generation here, matching the "real businesses have their own coding schemes" reasoning already applied to `Product.sku` and `Warehouse.code`.

### 2026-08-09 (8)

Completed

- Asset Register (second Asset Management module — the module's primary entity: one row per physical asset the business owns, tagged and classified)

Scope decision

- Checked existing migrations first: no `assets` table or `Asset` model existed. No collision with the Inventory module's `products`/`product_serials` (those track sellable stock and its serialised units; an asset is company property that is used, not sold).
- **Deliberately lean — identity and condition only, no purchase, assignment or location fields.** erp.txt's Asset Management checklist lists "Asset Purchase Information", "Asset Assignment" and "Asset Location Tracking" as three separate features immediately after this one, so cost/vendor/warranty, who holds the asset, and where it physically sits all belong to those modules rather than being crammed in here. Each will retrofit its own FK or child table onto `assets`, the same "build the dependency, then retrofit" pattern used repeatedly in this project (Customer Groups → `customers.customer_group_id`, Sales Targets → `sales_orders.assigned_to`). The create/edit form carries a footnote telling the admin exactly that, so the absence reads as deliberate rather than missing.
- **`asset_category_id` is nullable at the DB level with `nullOnDelete`, but required in the Form Request** — a documented, deliberate mismatch. Requiring it in validation means no asset can ever be filed without a category; making the column nullable means deleting a category cannot cascade away the register of physical property filed under it. An orphaned asset row is recoverable (re-file it); a cascade-deleted asset register is not. The DataTable renders such a row's category as a red "Uncategorised" so the condition is visible rather than silent. Verified directly in testing: deleting the category left the asset intact with `asset_category_id = NULL`.
- **`asset_code` is server-generated and immutable** — `'AST-' . str_pad(...)`, the same sequential numbering every other server-issued reference in this project uses (`CUST-`/`VEN-`/`JE-`/`AST-` is new and distinct). Unlike `AssetCategory.code` or `Warehouse.code` (both user-entered), an asset tag is physically affixed to the item, so `AssetService::update()` explicitly `unset()`s any submitted `asset_code` before writing — a re-issued tag would no longer match the sticker on the hardware. Verified in testing that a deliberately-submitted `asset_code` of "HACKED" was ignored and the original tag preserved.
- **Two independent state fields, matching this project's long-standing convention**: `asset_status` (`in_store`/`in_use`/`under_maintenance`/`disposed`) is the real lifecycle state, while `status` stays the boolean active/inactive archive toggle every module in this codebase has — the same separation `approval_status` vs `status` established in HRM and carried through every module since. `condition` (`new`/`good`/`fair`/`poor`) is a third, orthogonal axis (physical wear, not lifecycle), mirroring the `condition` enum `SalesReturnItem`/`GoodsReceiptItem`/`PurchaseReturnItem` already use.
- `serial_number` is nullable but unique — not every asset has a manufacturer serial, but no two may claim the same one. MySQL permits multiple NULLs under a unique index, so the nullable-and-unique combination behaves correctly; verified both an asset with a serial and one without saving cleanly side by side.

### 2026-08-09 (9)

Completed

- Asset Purchase Information (third Asset Management module — how, when, from whom and for how much each registered asset was acquired, plus its warranty window)

Scope decision

- **A separate one-to-one child table, not columns bolted onto `assets`.** erp.txt lists this as its own feature immediately after Asset Register, and Asset Register's own changelog entry explicitly reserved purchase data for it. Modelled on the `delivery_notes.delivery_id` precedent: a thin child record with a **unique** FK to its parent, `cascadeOnDelete` — one purchase record per asset, enforced at the DB level rather than only in validation. Keeping it out of `assets` also means an asset registered before its paperwork arrives is not forced to carry empty cost columns.
- **`vendor_id` and `purchase_order_id` are optional and `nullOnDelete`; `asset_id` is required and `cascadeOnDelete`.** A purchase record is meaningless without the asset it describes, so it goes when the asset goes — but it must survive a vendor or purchase order being deleted, since the historical fact of what was paid does not stop being true. Both behaviours verified directly in testing.
- **Reuses the Purchase module's existing `vendors` and `purchase_orders` tables via FK** rather than duplicating supplier data, exactly as the Naming/Table Conflict Guard directs for cross-module references.
- **`total_cost` is a computed accessor (`purchase_cost + additional_cost`), not a stored column** — a stored total would need rewriting whenever either component changed, giving two values that can disagree. Same reasoning as `SalesInvoice::balance_due`, `StockCountItem::variance` and `AssetCategory::depreciation_method_label`. `additional_cost` exists as its own field because freight/installation/setup is capitalised into an asset's book value but is not part of the invoice price — the Depreciation Calculation module will want the capitalised total, not the sticker price.
- **`is_under_warranty` is likewise computed, and is `false` (not `true`) when no expiry is recorded** — an asset with no warranty date has no warranty to be under, so an open-ended "true" would be wrong. The DataTable's warranty filter expresses the same three states as date comparisons (`>= today`, `< today`, `IS NULL`) rather than reading a stored flag, since none exists — the first filter in this project driven entirely by a computed condition.
- **The asset picker excludes assets that already have a purchase record**, with the current record's own asset added back on edit so the selection is never lost — the same `whereDoesntHave(...)->orWhere('id', ...)` technique `DeliveryNoteController` established for its own one-to-one relationship. Both branches verified in testing. The create form additionally shows an explanatory line when every asset is already recorded, rather than presenting an empty dropdown with no reason given.
- Added `Asset::assetPurchase(): HasOne` — the inverse relation, added because the picker's `whereDoesntHave` genuinely needs it, not speculatively (the same justification `Delivery::deliveryNote()` was added under).

- Updated `App\Models\Asset` — added `assetPurchase(): HasOne` and its `HasOne` import. No other change to the Asset Register module.

### 2026-08-09 (10)

Completed

- Asset Assignment (fourth Asset Management module — the record of which employee currently holds which asset, when it is due back, and what condition it went out and came back in)

Scope decision

- **FKs to the existing HRM `employees` table**, per the Naming/Table Conflict Guard's explicit instruction that Asset Management must reference `employees.id` rather than create a parallel staff table. `cascadeOnDelete` on both `asset_id` and `employee_id`, matching the convention every employee-scoped HRM child table (`attendances`, `leave_requests`, …) already uses.
- **A history table, not a single current-holder column on `assets`.** Every assignment and return is kept as its own row, so an asset's custody history survives the next handover — the alternative (a `current_employee_id` column) would overwrite the past on every reassignment. `assignment_status` (`assigned`/`returned`/`cancelled`) marks which row is the live one.
- **The one-holder-at-a-time rule is enforced in the Form Request, not the schema.** A physical asset can only be in one person's hands at once, but "no other row for this asset has `assignment_status = 'assigned'`" depends on the enum value of *other* rows and cannot be expressed as a DB unique constraint. `withValidator()` therefore runs the check and reports it naming the offending asset code and telling the admin to close the existing assignment first — the same app-level cross-record guard `ProductVariantRequest`'s duplicate-attribute-combination check established. The picker independently excludes assets already out, so the UI cannot offer a choice the validator would reject; both layers verified in testing.
- **`AssetAssignmentService` maintains `assets.asset_status`** — assigning sets `in_use`, returning/cancelling/deleting puts the asset back `in_store`. This is the same "one module's service maintains a status column another module owns" pattern already used by `SupplierQuotationService::markRfqVendorResponded()`, `PurchaseOrderService::markSupplierQuotationSelected()` and `BankReconciliationService`'s reconciled-flag handling. Three refinements beyond a naive implementation, each verified: **(1)** `releaseIfUnassigned()` only returns an asset to store once *no* open assignment still holds it, so closing one of several rows cannot wrongly free the asset; **(2)** moving an assignment to a different asset releases the one it left as well as claiming the new one; **(3)** an asset in `disposed` or `under_maintenance` is left alone entirely — those states are set deliberately elsewhere and must not be silently overwritten by an assignment record (verified: assigning a maintenance asset left it `under_maintenance`).
- **`is_overdue` is computed, not stored** — past its expected return date and still out. A stored flag would need a scheduled job to become true as the date passes, the same reasoning behind `TaxRate::is_current` and `AssetPurchase::is_under_warranty`. The DataTable's "Overdue Only" filter is therefore expressed as a date comparison on open assignments rather than a column lookup. Verified both ways: overdue while assigned, correctly false once returned.
- `condition_on_assign` is required and `condition_on_return` is nullable — the state it went out in is always known, the state it came back in only exists after a return. `returned_date` is `required_if:assignment_status,returned`, with the return fields hidden in the UI while the assignment is still open, mirroring the rule rather than showing fields that cannot yet apply.

Database

### 2026-08-09 (11)

Completed

- Employee Asset Tracking (fifth Asset Management module — who is holding which assets, read from the employee's side)

Scope decision

- **No new table, no Model, Service or Form Request.** Asset Assignment (built in the previous session) already records every handover and return against `employees.id`, so the data this checklist item calls for already exists — adding a second table would duplicate it and create two competing sources of truth. This module is therefore a pure read-only report, the same "controller only, one GET route, one Blade view" shape General Ledger, Cash Book, Accounts Receivable, Accounts Payable and the Accounting statements use. Per this project's established precedent it computes its own aggregation independently rather than sharing a service with `AssetAssignmentController`.
- **The distinction from Asset Assignment is the direction it reads.** Asset Assignment is the transactional CRUD screen, listed asset-first: one row per handover, with edit/delete actions. This module is employee-first and read-only: "what is this person holding, and what have they had before". The roadmap lists them as two separate features precisely because those are two different questions, and the Naming/Table Conflict Guard's instruction that this feature FK to the existing `employees` table is satisfied through the assignment records rather than by a new staff-linked table.
- **Two modes on one page**, the same shape General Ledger established and Cash Book/Accounts Receivable/Payable reuse: with no employee selected the page shows a per-employee summary (currently held, overdue, returned, lifetime); selecting one drills into their full record. Four organisation-wide stat tiles sit above both modes so the headline position is visible regardless of which one is showing.
- **Employees with no assignment history at all are excluded from the summary** — listing every employee on the payroll would bury the ones this report is about, the same "filter to rows with activity" refinement Accounts Receivable's own summary uses. The employee *filter dropdown* still lists everyone, so an admin can select someone and legitimately see "no assignment records for this employee".
- **`is_overdue` is read from the `AssetAssignment` model's existing accessor**, not recomputed here — it is already the single definition of "past its expected return date and still out", and duplicating the date comparison in this controller would risk the two drifting apart. This is the one place this module deliberately reuses rather than recomputes, because the value is a model concern, not a report aggregation.
- Detail rows are ordered `assigned` → `returned` → `cancelled` (via `orderByRaw("FIELD(...)")`, MySQL-specific and fine given the project's MySQL 8 stack) then by assignment date descending, so what someone is holding right now always sits at the top of their record rather than being buried under history.

### 2026-08-09 (12)

Completed

- Asset Location Tracking (sixth Asset Management module — where each asset physically sits, with full movement history; built as **two coupled pieces** in one module, per the Pricing Management precedent: an Asset Locations master and the Movement tracking screen that uses it)

Scope decision

- **Two coupled pieces, one module.** A movement record needs somewhere to move *to*, so a locations master had to exist; splitting them into two roadmap items would have left either half unusable on its own. This follows the documented Pricing Management precedent (Price Tiers + Product Prices shipped together as one checklist item), including the cross-link buttons in each screen's toolbar so an admin can move between them without going through the sidebar.
- **A new `asset_locations` master rather than reusing Inventory's `warehouses`.** Considered reusing them, but a warehouse in this project is stock-storage for sellable product; assets sit in offices, branches, floors and rooms, which `warehouses` has no vocabulary for. `location_type` includes a `warehouse` value so a business that does keep assets in one can still classify it that way. Per the Naming/Table Conflict Guard, `department_id` FKs to the **existing HRM `departments`** table rather than creating a second departments list.
- **Current location is the latest movement, not a stored `is_current` flag.** A flag would have to be flipped across sibling rows on every insert, edit and delete, and could silently end up with two "current" rows or none. `AssetLocationMovement::is_current` therefore compares against the latest row for that asset, and `Asset::currentLocationMovement()` uses `latestOfMany(['moved_date', 'id'])` — tie-broken by id so two movements dated the same day still resolve to one deterministic answer.
- **A bug was caught and fixed during verification**: that relation was first written as `latestOfMany(['moved_date' => 'max', 'id' => 'max'])`, which Laravel interprets as a column literally named `max`, producing `Unknown column 'asset_location_movements.max'`. The correct multi-column form is a plain list of columns. Caught by the smoke test before the module was reported complete, then re-verified end to end.
- **The "Current Location Only" list filter is a correlated subquery, not a column lookup** — for the same reason there is no stored flag. It selects `MAX(id)` per asset among rows sharing that asset's own `MAX(moved_date)`, so exactly one row per asset survives even when two movements share a date. Verified directly through the AJAX endpoint: three movements across two assets correctly reduced to two rows, each the right one.
- **Re-recording the location an asset is already in is rejected** — it adds no information and would clutter the history. Deliberately checked against only the *latest* movement, so an asset legitimately returning to a previous location is still allowed; both behaviours verified.
- **`asset_location_id` is `cascadeOnDelete`, not `nullOnDelete`** — unlike most optional FKs in this project, a movement whose destination is unknown says nothing at all, so the history goes with the location. This is called out in the location edit form's footnote so an admin deleting a location knows what else goes with it. `moved_by` is nullable `nullOnDelete` and set server-side from the authenticated admin, never client-submitted, the same pattern as `RelationshipHistory.created_by`.

- Added one migration (`database/migrations/2026_08_09_140000_create_asset_locations_table.php`) creating both tables:
  - `asset_locations`: `name`; `code` unique; `location_type` enum (`office`/`branch`/`warehouse`/`site`/`other`) default `office`; `department_id` nullable → `departments.id`, `nullOnDelete`; `building`/`floor`/`room` nullable; `address`/`description` nullable text; `status` boolean.
  - `asset_location_movements`: `asset_id` → `assets.id` `cascadeOnDelete`; `asset_location_id` → `asset_locations.id` `cascadeOnDelete`; `moved_date` required date; `moved_by` nullable → `admins.id` `nullOnDelete`; `reason`/`notes` nullable text; `status` boolean.

Models

- Added `App\Models\AssetLocation` — `public const LOCATION_TYPES`; `status` cast boolean; `getPlacementAttribute()` (folds building/floor/room into one readable line, omitting the parts not recorded, returning `null` when none are); relations `department()`, `movements()`; `scopeActive()`.
- Added `App\Models\AssetLocationMovement` — casts `moved_date` to `date`; `getIsCurrentAttribute()` (described above); relations `asset()`, `assetLocation()`, `movedBy()` (→ `Admin` via `moved_by`); `scopeActive()`.
- Updated `App\Models\Asset` — added `locationMovements(): HasMany` and `currentLocationMovement(): HasOne`, both needed by this module's screens and by the current-location display.

No cross-table side effects: unlike Asset Assignment (which maintains `assets.asset_status`), a location move does not change the asset's lifecycle state — an asset in use stays in use wherever it sits.

- Added `App\Http\Requests\Admin\AssetLocationMovementRequest` — `asset_id`/`asset_location_id` required `exists:` checks; `moved_date` required date; `reason`/`notes` nullable; `status` required boolean; `moved_by` deliberately absent (server-set). `withValidator()` holds the same-location rejection described above, correctly excluding the record being edited from its own check.

- Added `App\Http\Controllers\Admin\AssetLocationMovementController` — standard CRUD, module string `asset-location-movements`; index eager-loads `asset`/`assetLocation`/`movedBy`, adds `asset_location_id`, `asset_id` and the correlated-subquery `current_only` filters; search matches the asset's `name`/`asset_code` or the location's `name`/`code`; default sort `moved_date DESC, id DESC`. Columns: `asset_name`, `location_name` (code and placement as the subtitle), `moved_date_formatted`, `current_badge` (green Current / grey History), `moved_by_name`, `status_badge`. `store()` injects `moved_by` from the authenticated admin. ### 2026-08-09 (13)

Completed

- Maintenance Schedule (seventh Asset Management module — planned recurring or one-off maintenance per asset, with the next due date derived rather than typed)

Scope decision

- **This module is the plan; Maintenance History (the next roadmap item) will be the record of work actually done.** The split is kept clean: a schedule says what should happen and when it is next due, and carries `last_performed_date` as the anchor the next due date counts from. When Maintenance History is built it will presumably write completed jobs and push that date forward, at which point the schedule rolls itself — the same "build the dependency, then retrofit" pattern used throughout this project. No history table or completion action is invented here.
- **`next_due_date` is always derived by the service and is deliberately absent from the Form Request.** A user-typed due date could silently contradict the frequency, and the two would then drift apart on every edit. `calculateNextDueDate()` counts forward from `last_performed_date`, falling back to `start_date` when the job has never been done — so a brand-new schedule is due on its start date, and one performed last week is due one interval after that. Verified across quarterly (2026-07-05 → 2026-10-05) and yearly (2025-03-10 → 2026-03-10).
- **A one-time schedule is handled as its own case, not as an interval of zero**: due on its start date while unperformed, and with **no** due date at all once performed — it is finished, not overdue forever. Verified both states.
- **Only an `active` schedule can be due.** `is_due`/`is_overdue` return false for paused, completed and cancelled schedules regardless of the date, so pausing a schedule genuinely silences it rather than leaving it screaming in the overdue list. Verified with a paused schedule whose date was months past.
- **`days_until_due` is signed** — negative once overdue — so one accessor carries both "how long left" and "how late", and the list column reads "in N day(s)" or "Overdue by N day(s)" off the same value. All three of these are computed accessors, not stored columns, for the same reason as `TaxRate::is_current` and `AssetAssignment::is_overdue`: a stored flag would need a scheduled job to become true as dates pass.
- **Two optional responsible parties, not one**: `assigned_to` FKs to the existing HRM `employees` table (internal technician) per the Naming/Table Conflict Guard, and `vendor_id` to `vendors` (external servicer). Real maintenance is sometimes done in-house, sometimes contracted out, and occasionally both — collapsing them into one field would have forced a false choice. Both are `nullOnDelete`, so losing a vendor or employee record does not destroy the schedule.
- An asset may carry **any number of schedules** — servicing, inspection and calibration are different jobs on the same machine — so unlike Asset Assignment nothing is excluded from the picker beyond disposed assets, which have nothing left to maintain.

### 2026-08-09 (14)

Completed

- Maintenance History (eighth Asset Management module — the record of maintenance work actually carried out, and the piece that closes the loop Maintenance Schedule was built to expect)

Scope decision

- **This is the counterpart to Maintenance Schedule**: that module says what should happen and when it is next due; this one records what was done. The link is `asset_maintenance_schedule_id`, and completing a job here pushes the schedule's `last_performed_date` forward, which re-derives its `next_due_date` through the schedule service — exactly the integration the previous module's changelog entry anticipated, now implemented rather than assumed.
- **The schedule is recalculated from scratch on every write, not stamped forward.** `syncSchedule()` finds the most recent *completed* record for that schedule and rebuilds `last_performed_date` and `next_due_date` from it. Stamping forward would be simpler but would leave the schedule stuck at a date no surviving record supports the moment a record is edited, cancelled, moved or deleted. Every one of those reversals was verified: completing a later job moved the due date forward, deleting it fell back to the earlier completed job, and deleting the last one reset `last_performed_date` to null and the schedule back to falling due on its start date.
- **Only `completed` work moves a schedule.** An `in_progress` or `cancelled` record is real history worth keeping but is not evidence the job is done — verified that logging an in-progress job dated later than the last completed one left the due date untouched, and that flipping it to completed then moved it.
- **Moving a record between schedules recalculates both** — the one it left as well as the one it joined — the same two-sided correction `AssetAssignmentService` applies when an assignment changes asset.
- **`asset_maintenance_schedule_id` is optional and `nullOnDelete`.** Unplanned repairs have no schedule behind them at all, and a completed job stays a valid historical record even if the schedule it came from is later removed. The list exposes this directly as a Planned / Unplanned "origin" filter and badge.
- **A record cannot be logged against a schedule belonging to a different asset** — that would silently move the wrong schedule's due date. Enforced in the Form Request naming the problem in plain language, and independently in the create/edit form, where the schedule dropdown narrows to the selected asset (with "Unplanned" always available) and clears itself if the current selection no longer applies.
- `maintenance_type` adds a **`repair`** value the schedule enum does not have: you plan preventive work, but you record unplanned repairs. The two enums are deliberately not shared for that reason.

### 2026-08-09 (15)

Completed

- Depreciation Calculation (ninth Asset Management module — accumulated depreciation and net book value per asset, plus a year-by-year schedule)

Scope decision

- **No new table, no Model, Service or Form Request.** Every input already exists: the capitalised cost comes from Asset Purchase Information (`total_cost`, itself an accessor), and the method, useful life and salvage percentage come from the asset's category — which has carried them since Asset Categories was built, where the changelog entry said plainly that "the Depreciation Calculation module will read them". Storing computed depreciation would create figures that drift the moment a cost or a category setting is corrected, so everything is derived on read, the same "controller only" shape every report in this project uses.
- **Two modes on one page**, the shape General Ledger established and Employee Asset Tracking reused: the list shows every asset's position as of the chosen date; selecting one asset additionally shows its full year-by-year schedule above the list.
- **Assets that cannot be depreciated are reported, not hidden.** An asset with no purchase record, no category, a category set to `none`, or no useful life appears in the list with the reason stated in place of the method — and is excluded from the totals rather than being counted as worth zero. A `none`-method asset still shows its cost as its book value, because land does not lose value by sitting there. Verified all four cases.
- **Straight line** spreads `cost − salvage` evenly over the life; the year-by-year schedule therefore lands exactly on the salvage value in the final year (verified: 10,000 cost with 10% salvage over 5 years → 1,800/year, closing at exactly 1,000).
- **Reducing balance uses the double-declining rate (2 ÷ life)** applied to the written-down value each year, floored at salvage. The obvious alternative — deriving a rate from the salvage percentage — is mathematically undefined when salvage is zero, which is the common case here, so one well-known convention is used throughout and stated plainly on screen (the detail header prints the actual rate) rather than being hidden or made configurable.
- **Elapsed time is fractional, not whole years**, so an asset bought mid-year shows a proportionate charge rather than jumping a full year at a time; it is floored at zero so a future-dated purchase never shows negative depreciation. Accumulated depreciation is capped at the depreciable amount, so a fully-depreciated asset rests at its salvage value instead of going negative — flagged in the list as "Fully depreciated".

Database

- **No new tables** — reads `assets`, `asset_purchases` and `asset_categories`, all already built. Confirmed `php artisan migrate` was not needed.

Models

- No new or modified models. `Asset::assetCategory()` and `Asset::assetPurchase()` (both pre-existing) are eager-loaded together.

Services / Requests

- None — read-only report, per the established report-controller pattern. The three filters are optional `GET` parameters read directly off the `Request`.

Controllers

- Added `App\Http\Controllers\Admin\AssetDepreciationController` — `index()` reads `asset_id`/`asset_category_id`/`as_of_date` (defaulting to today), maps every matching asset through `buildRow()`, and sums cost/accumulated/book value across **only** the depreciable rows. `buildRow()` resolves the four not-depreciable cases before doing any arithmetic and returns a uniform shape either way. `straightLine()` and `reducingBalance()` hold the two methods, each returning `[accumulated, annual charge]`; `reducingBalance()` walks year by year so a partial final year is charged proportionately and the salvage floor is respected at each step. `buildSchedule()` produces the per-year table for a single selected asset, labelling each period from the purchase anniversary rather than the calendar year, since depreciation runs from the purchase date.

Views

- Added `resources/views/admin/asset-depreciation/index.blade.php` — a full-page (non-modal) report view with 4 `.stat-card` tiles (Total Cost, Accumulated Depreciation, Net Book Value, and a Depreciating-assets count that shows "n / total" only when some assets are excluded). The optional schedule card sits above the list and its subtitle states the method, life, cost, salvage amount and percentage — and, for reducing balance, the actual rate being applied. The main table's Method column carries the not-depreciable reason in red where applicable, and its `<tfoot>` totals row is labelled "Totals (depreciating assets)" so the figures are not mistaken for covering every row. Asset names link through to their own schedule, carrying the chosen date forward.

### 2026-08-09 (16)

Completed

- Disposal Management (tenth Asset Management module — taking an asset out of service, with the book value and gain or loss snapshotted at disposal)

Scope decision

- **One disposal per asset, enforced at the DB level** via a unique `asset_id` — the same one-to-one shape `asset_purchases` uses. An asset is bought once and disposed of once; the picker excludes assets that already have a record, with the edited record's own asset added back so the selection is never lost.
- **`book_value_at_disposal` and `gain_loss` are stored snapshots, not derived figures** — the deliberate opposite of the Depreciation Calculation module, which computes everything live. A disposal is a historical financial event: correcting an asset's cost or its category's useful life next year must not silently rewrite what a sale two years ago was worth. This mirrors the same split already made between Sales Commission (stored snapshot) and Sales Target (live accessor), and is documented in the service and in the migration.
- **The book-value calculation is recomputed here rather than shared with the Depreciation controller.** It follows the same documented conventions — straight line over `cost − salvage`, or double-declining (2 ÷ life) floored at salvage — consistent with this project's standing rule that each module owns its own calculation. Verified that the two agree: the same asset showed a book value of 6,400 in both modules.
- **The service maintains `assets.asset_status`**, the same cross-module status pattern `AssetAssignmentService` established: a `completed` disposal marks the asset `disposed`, and moving it to pending/cancelled, changing it to a different asset, or deleting the record puts the asset back. `restoreAsset()` only acts on assets currently marked `disposed` and only once no other completed disposal still stands, so it cannot wrongly resurrect something. Restoring returns the asset to `in_store` rather than to whatever state it held before — that earlier state is recorded nowhere, and a known-safe default beats a guess. All four transitions verified.
- **A disposal cannot predate the purchase.** Enforced in the Form Request against the linked purchase record, with the actual purchase date quoted back in the message.
- `disposal_method` covers the six realistic outcomes (`sold`/`scrapped`/`donated`/`written_off`/`traded_in`/`lost`); a scrapped or lost asset simply has zero proceeds, so the loss equals its remaining book value — verified (proceeds 0 against a 6,400 book value produced exactly −6,400).

Scope decision

- **One deliberate, documented exception to the "each module computes its own aggregation" rule**: net book value is taken from `AssetDisposalService::bookValueAt()`, which was made public in the previous module *specifically* so this one would not become a third copy of the depreciation convention. Duplicating that arithmetic a third time would have been the one place where the rule stopped paying for itself — three copies drifting is materially worse than two. Everything else on the page is counted locally.
- **Book value covers only assets still on the books.** A disposed asset has already been accounted for through its disposal record, so including it would double-count; accumulated depreciation is therefore derived as live cost less live book value rather than across the whole register.

Nothing here is a historical financial event, so nothing is snapshotted.
- `email` is nullable but unique — not every client has one on file, but two clients must not claim the same address. MySQL permits multiple NULLs under a unique index, so nullable-and-unique behaves correctly; verified with one client holding an email and another with none.

### 2026-08-10

Completed

- Projects (second Project Management module — the module's primary entity: a delivery engagement run for a client, with schedule, ownership, priority and state)

Scope decision

- **No budget column.** "Project Budgets" is its own checklist item immediately after this one and will attach through `project_id`, the same "build the dependency, then retrofit" pattern used throughout this project. Putting a budget figure on `projects` now would have made that module either redundant or contradictory.
- **`client_id` is nullable at the DB level with `nullOnDelete`, but required in the Form Request** — the same deliberate, documented split `assets.asset_category_id` already uses. Requiring it in validation means no project can be filed without a client; making the column nullable means deleting a client cannot cascade away the delivery history run for them. The list renders such a row's client as a red "Client removed" so the condition is visible rather than silent. Verified: deleting the client left the project intact with `client_id = NULL`.
- **`department_id` FKs the existing HRM `departments` table and `project_manager_id` the existing `employees` table**, per the Naming/Table Conflict Guard — no parallel staff or department tables. Both are optional and `nullOnDelete`; a project survives losing its owning department or manager.
- **`progress_percent` is a stored column, deliberately, and this is the one place the project's usual "derive anything derivable" preference does not apply yet** — there is nothing to derive it from until the Tasks module exists. It is maintained manually for now, noted as such in the migration; when Tasks is built it can either feed this column or supersede it with a computed accessor.
- **`is_overdue`, `days_remaining` and `duration_days` are computed accessors**, not stored. A stored overdue flag would need a scheduled job to become true as the date passes (the same reasoning as `AssetAssignment::is_overdue` / `TaxRate::is_current`), and `days_remaining` is signed — negative once late — so one value carries both "how long left" and "how late", which the timeline column reads off directly. All three return `null`/`false` for a completed or cancelled project: neither can be late any more, expressed as a shared `Project::CLOSED_STATUSES` constant used by both the model and the controller's overdue filter so the two can never disagree.
- **The service owns completion consistency, not the form.** `withDerivedFields()` forces `progress_percent` to 100 and stamps `actual_end_date` (defaulting to today) when a project is marked completed, and clears `actual_end_date` again when a project is moved back off completed — so the field can never claim a project finished on a day it did not. The create/edit form mirrors this client-side (hides Progress and reveals Actual End Date on completion) using the established `MutationObserver`-on-remote-modal technique, but the server is authoritative. Both directions verified.
- **`project_code` is server-generated and immutable** — `'PRJ-' . str_pad(...)`, a new prefix distinct from every other reference number in this project. `update()` strips any submitted code, since every future task, timesheet and invoice will reference it. Verified: an injected code of "HACKED" was ignored.
