### 2026-08-10 (2)

Completed

- Project Budgets (third Project Management module — a project's planned spend, broken into budget lines by category, versioned per project)

Scope decision

- **Header + line items**, the established master-detail shape (`PriceListService`/`ProductBundleService`'s delete-then-recreate `syncItems()`), because a budget is only meaningful as a breakdown: a single lump figure on `projects` would tell nobody where the money is going, and Project Profitability Reports will want the categories.
- **Versioned per project, not one-to-one.** A project routinely carries an original budget and later revisions, so `project_budgets` is not a unique child of `projects` the way `asset_purchases` is of `assets`. Uniqueness is `(project_id, version)` (named index `pbudget_project_version_unique`), and `ProjectBudgetService::nextVersion()` derives the version from that project's own highest — not a global counter. Verified: a second budget on the same project came out as v2 while the first budget on a different project correctly started at v1, and a hand-inserted duplicate version was rejected by the DB.
- **`total_amount` is a stored, server-computed column, not an accessor** — a deliberate departure from this module's usual "derive anything derivable" preference and the one place it should not apply: a budget is an approved planning figure, so the total that was signed off must not silently re-shape itself. It is summed from the submitted lines by the service on every write and is absent from the Form Request, so it can never be client-supplied. Same reasoning as every other document total in this project (`sales_quotations.grand_total`).
- **`budget_code` and `version` are owned by the service and stripped on update**, along with `project_id` — moving a budget to another project would renumber it against a different version sequence, so the edit form shows the project read-only and submits it as a hidden field purely to satisfy validation. Verified: an injected `budget_code` of "HACKED", a `version` of 99 and a different `project_id` were all ignored.
- **The service owns approval consistency.** Setting the state to `approved` stamps `approved_date` (today if none given); moving it back off `approved` clears both `approved_date` and `approved_by`, so a budget can never claim it was signed off on a day it was not — the same shape `ProjectService`'s completion handling uses. The form mirrors it by hiding the approval fields unless the state is Approved; the server is authoritative. Both directions verified.
- **`category` is a fixed enum** (`labour`/`materials`/`equipment`/`subcontract`/`travel`/`software`/`other`), not a lookup table — erp.txt lists no "Budget Categories" feature, and this matches the "hardcoded enum now, retrofit only on a real need" choice made repeatedly in this project.
- **Naming note, documented rather than left to collide later**: roadmap item 13 (Budget & Finance) also lists a "Project Budget" feature. That is company-wide budget planning and will own its own tables; `project_budgets`/`project_budget_items` belong to Project Management and are the per-project planning figures Project Profitability Reports will read. Written into the migration as a comment as well as here.
- No spent/variance columns — there is nothing to compare against until Project Expenses and Time Tracking exist. Those figures belong to the reports that will read both sides, not to the budget record.

### 2026-08-10 (3)

Completed

- Project Teams (fourth Project Management module — who is on a project, in what role, for how much of their time, and over what period)

Scope decision

- **A flat membership table, not a team header + members.** The project already is the header, so a separate "team" record would add a level carrying nothing of its own. One row per employee per project, with joined/left dates holding the history of who was on it and when — the same structural family as `AssetAssignment` rather than the master-detail shape Project Budgets uses.
- **`employee_id` FKs the existing HRM `employees` table** per the Naming/Table Conflict Guard — no parallel staff table. Both `project_id` and `employee_id` are `cascadeOnDelete`: a membership row means nothing without either side of it, verified in both directions.
- **`(project_id, employee_id)` is unique** (named index `ptm_project_employee_unique`) — someone is either on a project or not; a change of role or allocation edits the existing row rather than stacking a second one. Mirrored in the Form Request so the admin gets "edit the existing record instead" rather than a raw constraint error. Verified that the same employee can still legitimately sit on a *different* project.
- **`is_current` is a computed accessor** — no departure date recorded, or one that has not arrived yet. A stored flag would need a scheduled job to flip as a future leaving date passes, the same reasoning behind `Project::is_overdue` and `TaxRate::is_current`. The list's Current/Past filter is therefore expressed as the same date comparison, exposed once as `scopeCurrent()` so the model, the controller filter and the lead rule below can never disagree about what "still on the team" means.
- **One current lead per project, enforced in the Form Request.** This is not a uniqueness constraint any index can express — it depends on the enum value *and* the leaving dates of other rows — so `withValidator()` checks it and names the sitting lead in the message ("This project already has a team lead (Lead One). Change their role or record their leaving date first."). Only *current* members count: once the sitting lead's leaving date is recorded, the slot frees up. Both halves verified directly.
- **`allocation_percent` is per-project, capped 0.01–100**, and deliberately **not** validated against an employee's total allocation across all their projects. Over-allocation is a real management question, but flagging it belongs in a capacity report reading across projects (and against Time Tracking, which does not exist yet) — silently blocking a legitimate 60/60 split at data-entry time would be the wrong call. Flagged here so a future capacity view knows the figure is unconstrained across projects.
- `team_role` is a fixed enum (`lead`/`member`/`analyst`/`developer`/`designer`/`tester`/`consultant`/`support`) rather than a lookup table — erp.txt lists no "Team Roles" master, and this is the same "hardcoded enum now, retrofit only on a real need" choice made repeatedly in this project. It is a project-specific role, independent of the employee's HRM `designation`, which the list shows alongside it.

- **No inverse `teamMembers(): HasMany` was added on `Project`** — nothing built in this task needs it, the same "avoid speculative relations" reasoning applied throughout this project.

No cross-table side effects: unlike `AssetAssignmentService` (which maintains `assets.asset_status`), joining a project team changes nothing on the project or the employee record — a project's own state is set deliberately on its own screen.

### 2026-08-10 (4)

Completed

- Milestones (fifth Project Management module — the dated checkpoints a project is delivered against)

Scope decision

- **Flat per-project records, sequenced by `sort_order`** — the project is the header, so no separate "milestone plan" level. New milestones land at the end of their own project's sequence via `nextSortOrder()`, which reads that project's own highest rather than a global count (the same per-parent numbering `ProjectBudgetService::nextVersion()` uses). The order field is exposed but optional; leaving it blank auto-places.
- **Deliberately carries no billing amount.** Milestone-based billing is common, but "Project Billing" is its own checklist item and will attach through `milestone_id` if the client bills that way — putting an amount here now would either duplicate that module or contradict it. Same discipline applied when Projects deliberately omitted a budget figure.
- **Names are unique within their own project**, not globally (`pms_project_name_unique` on `(project_id, name)`, mirrored in the Form Request) — two projects may each legitimately have a "Phase 1". Verified both halves: a duplicate within one project is rejected, the same name on another project is accepted.
- **`is_overdue`, `days_remaining` and `was_on_time` are computed accessors**, not stored. A stored overdue flag would need a scheduled job to become true as the due date passes (the same reasoning as `Project::is_overdue`), and `days_remaining` is signed so one value carries both "how long left" and "how late". `was_on_time` compares the completion date against the due date and returns **null** while the milestone is still open — there is nothing to judge yet, so null rather than a misleading false. The first two fall silent for a completed or cancelled milestone, expressed as a shared `ProjectMilestone::CLOSED_STATUSES` constant used by both the model and the controller's overdue filter so the two can never disagree.
- **The service owns completion consistency**: marking a milestone completed stamps `completed_date` (today if none given), and moving it back off completed clears that date again, so it can never claim it was delivered on a day it was not. The form mirrors this by revealing the completion date field only for the completed state; the server is authoritative. Both directions verified, including a deliberate early completion (on time) and a late one.
- **`assigned_to` is optional and `nullOnDelete`, FKing the existing HRM `employees` table** per the Naming/Table Conflict Guard — losing the owner must not delete the milestone, verified. `project_id` is `cascadeOnDelete`: a milestone has no meaning without its project.
- **Sorted soonest-due first** (`due_date`, then `sort_order`), with client-side ordering disabled — this is a delivery worklist rather than a log, the same ordering choice the Maintenance Schedule screen made and the opposite of Maintenance History's.

Database

### 2026-08-10 (5)

Completed

- Tasks (sixth Project Management module — the unit of work on a project, and the record the next four checklist items all read)

Scope decision

- **Table is `project_tasks`, not a bare `tasks`.** A generic `tasks` table is exactly the name a later module (Support tickets, workflow to-dos) would plausibly want, so it is namespaced to its own module in the spirit of the Naming/Table Conflict Guard. Model `ProjectTask`, routes/permissions/menu all `project-task(s)`.
- **Deliberately carries no dependency link and no logged time.** "Task Dependencies" and "Time Tracking" are their own checklist items and will attach through `task_id`; `estimated_hours` here is the *plan*, and actual hours belong to Time Tracking. This is the same discipline applied when Projects omitted a budget and Milestones omitted a billing amount.
- **`sort_order` is the position within a board column**, auto-placed at the end of that project's own list by `nextSortOrder()` (per-project, not a global counter — the same technique `ProjectMilestoneService` and `ProjectBudgetService` use). Task Board Kanban will reorder it; nothing in this module does.
- **`project_milestone_id` is optional and `nullOnDelete`** — plenty of work hangs off no milestone at all, and deleting a milestone must not delete the work done under it. `project_id` is `cascadeOnDelete` (a task means nothing without its project) and `assigned_to` is optional `nullOnDelete`, FKing the existing HRM `employees` table per the Naming/Table Conflict Guard. All three behaviours verified.
- **A task can only hang off a milestone of its own project** — enforced in `withValidator()` naming the problem plainly, because a cross-project milestone would make the milestone view silently show foreign work. The form independently narrows the milestone dropdown to the selected project (and clears a selection that no longer applies), so the UI cannot offer what the validator would reject — the same two-layer approach `AssetMaintenanceRecordController` uses for its schedule picker.
- **`is_overdue` and `days_remaining` are computed accessors**, not stored — a stored flag would need a scheduled job to become true as the due date passes (same reasoning as `Project::is_overdue`). Both fall silent for a done or cancelled task via the shared `ProjectTask::CLOSED_STATUSES` constant, which the controller's overdue filter and the new `scopeOpen()` also use, so no two places can disagree about what "still open" means. A task with no due date is never overdue — verified.
- **The service owns completion consistency**: marking a task Done forces progress to 100 and stamps `completed_date` (today if none given); reopening clears that date. The form mirrors it (hides Progress, reveals Completed Date on Done); the server is authoritative. Both directions verified.
- **`task_code` is server-generated and immutable** (`TSK-000001`, a new prefix) and stripped on update, since Time Tracking, Timesheets and Task Dependencies will all reference it. Verified: an injected code of "HACKED" was ignored.
- `progress_percent` is stored and manually maintained for the same reason `Project::progress_percent` is — there is nothing to derive it from until Time Tracking exists.

### 2026-08-10 (6)

Completed

- Task Board Kanban (seventh Project Management module — a drag-and-drop board view over the tasks built in the previous step)

Scope decision

- **No new table, no Model, no Form Request.** Tasks already carry `task_status` (the column) and `sort_order` (the position within it — reserved for exactly this when Tasks was built), so the board is a second way of looking at `project_tasks`, the same relationship the Sales Pipeline Kanban has to Opportunities.
- **Deliberately not the standard DataTable + modal pattern.** A board is a live, single-screen interaction, so it follows the documented Kanban/POS precedent instead: a full-page non-modal view, plain `GET` filters, vanilla HTML5 drag-and-drop, and a small JSON move endpoint. This is a genuinely different interaction model, not a stylistic departure.
- **No new JS dependency.** Drag-and-drop, drop-position calculation, optimistic movement, rollback and the toast are all hand-written in `task-board.js` — the same "no new dependency for one screen" choice made for the Opportunities Kanban, Chart.js-via-CDN and JsBarcode.
- **Optimistic with rollback.** A card moves the instant it is dropped, then the move is saved; if the server rejects it the card is put back exactly where it came from (including its position among its siblings) and a red toast explains why, so the board can never quietly disagree with the database. Verified by exercising the endpoint directly, including a rejected invalid state.
- **Drop position is honoured, not just the column.** The drop handler works out where the card sits relative to its neighbours and posts the column's full id list top-to-bottom; the service renumbers `sort_order` to match what the user actually sees. The renumbering is scoped to the moved task's own project, so a board showing several projects cannot renumber another project's tasks. Verified: after dropping one card below another, their `sort_order` values came back 1 and 2 in the visible order.
- **Done handling is not duplicated.** `moveToStatus()` routes through the existing `withDerivedFields()`, so dropping a card into Done stamps its completion date and forces progress to 100 exactly as the form does, and dragging it back out clears the date again. Both verified, and the response returns the server's own progress figure so the card's bar updates without a reload.
- **One deliberate change to an existing module, as permitted and documented**: `ProjectTaskService` gained `moveToStatus()`. A board drag only ever changes state and position, so it routes through a small dedicated method rather than the full update path — the same reasoning behind `OpportunityService::updateStage()` and `ActivityService::updateActivityStatus()`. Nothing else in the Tasks module was touched; its migration, model, request, controller, views and JS are unchanged.
- **Custom CSS was added, scoped to this screen** in a `@push('styles')` block (the same technique the Opportunities Kanban, Holidays Calendar and every report page use) — no shared stylesheet was edited, so nothing elsewhere in the app can be affected. The board uses accent-driven columns, priority-coloured card borders, initials avatars, inline progress bars, overdue dates in red, hover elevation, a drop-target highlight, a toast, and a mobile breakpoint that narrows columns to 82vw. Colours are drawn from Bootstrap CSS variables with literal fallbacks, so the board follows the app's own theme.
- **Permissions are `.view` and `.move`**, not the CRUD four — the board creates and deletes nothing. Same custom-verb precedent as `pos.checkout`/`pos.void` and `payroll.mark-paid`.

Database

- **No new tables** — reads and writes `project_tasks` only. `php artisan migrate` reported "Nothing to migrate".

Models

- No new or modified models.

Services

- `App\Services\ProjectTaskService` — added `moveToStatus(ProjectTask $task, string $status, array $orderedIds = [])`, described above. This is the only change to an existing module in this step.

Controllers

- Added `App\Http\Controllers\Admin\TaskBoardController` — `index()` loads active tasks (optionally filtered by project, assignee or priority), groups them into one collection per `ProjectTask::STATUSES` value ordered by `sort_order`, and derives the three header figures (total, overdue via the model's own accessor, unassigned). `move()` validates the target state against the same constant and the id list as integers, calls the service, logs a readable "moved from X to Y" entry via `ActivityLogger`, and returns the new state plus the server's progress figure as JSON. Both wrapped in the standard `DB::beginTransaction()` shape.

Views

- Added `resources/views/admin/task-board/index.blade.php` — a full-page (non-modal) board. A `GET` filter bar (Project, Assignee, Priority, each submitting on change) with a Clear link shown only when a filter is active, three inline stat pills (with the overdue pill turning red when non-zero) and a List View link back to Tasks. One column per state with an icon, accent underline and live count; cards show the task code, a priority pill, the title, project and milestone chip, an optional progress bar, an initials avatar or "Unassigned", and the due date in red when overdue, plus a hover-revealed shortcut that opens that task in the list view pre-searched by its code. Empty columns render a dashed "Nothing here yet" placeholder rather than a blank gap. All styling lives in a scoped `@push('styles')` block; the move-route template is handed to JS via a `window` variable, the same technique the Opportunities Kanban and Product Images screens use.
- Added `public/assets/system/js/pages/task-board.js` — drag-and-drop binding, `cardAfterPoint()` for the drop position, `orderedIds()` for the column payload, `refreshCounts()` (which also adds or removes the empty-state placeholder), `persist()` and `rollback()`, and a small toast helper. CSRF is handled by the project's existing global `$.ajaxSetup` header, so no per-request token wiring was needed.

Routes

Placed directly after the Tasks block.

Inserted live via `Permission::firstOrCreate(['name' => ..., 'guard_name' => 'admin'])` and synced onto "Super Admin" via tinker per established precedent (the seeder is still not idempotent and was not re-run wholesale).

### 2026-08-10 (7)

Completed

- Gantt Chart (eighth Project Management module — a read-only timeline over the projects, milestones and tasks already built)

Scope decision

- **No new table, no Model, no Service, no Form Request** — Projects, Milestones and Tasks all carry their own dates; this schedules them on one axis. The same "controller only, one GET route, one Blade view" shape every read-only screen in this project uses, and per the standing precedent it computes its own aggregation rather than sharing a service.
- **No charting library.** The whole chart is CSS-positioned `<div>`s driven by server-computed percentages — the same "no new dependency for one screen" choice made for the Opportunities Kanban, the Task Board and JsBarcode/Chart.js-via-CDN. A Gantt library would also have meant a build step this project does not have.
- **Two modes on one page**, the shape General Ledger established and Cash Book/Employee Asset Tracking reuse: with no project selected every active project is plotted on its own span (each row links through to its own timeline); selecting one plots that project's tasks instead, with its milestones marked on a dedicated axis row.
- **All positioning is server-side.** The controller resolves the axis from the data (padded out to whole months), then hands every row an `offset`/`width` percentage, so the view contains no arithmetic and the numbers can be tested directly — which they were.
- **A dated off-by-one was caught and fixed during verification.** The first implementation mixed `endOfMonth()` (23:59:59) into day counts, so the month header blocks summed to **103.27%** and overran the axis. Every span in the class is now normalised to midnight and measured against one shared `totalDays()` helper (inclusive of both ends), after which the month blocks sum to 100% and a task falling on the very last day of the range ends at exactly 100%. Both re-verified numerically.
- **Undated work is reported, not silently dropped.** A task with neither a start nor a due date cannot be plotted, so it is excluded from the chart and listed underneath in an amber "not on the chart" panel naming each item — the same "say what is missing" approach Stock Valuation takes with missing costs and Financial Reports with draft entries.
- **An open-ended row is drawn as such**: a task or project with no end date is plotted from its start with a dashed, square-ended bar, rather than being given a fabricated finish date.
- Bars are coloured by state (task states in project mode, project states in overview), outlined in red when overdue, and filled to their progress percentage; milestones are diamonds on the axis (green when completed, red when overdue); today is a vertical red line, drawn only when it falls inside the plotted range.

Database

- **No new tables** — reads `projects`, `project_milestones` and `project_tasks`. `php artisan migrate` was not needed.

Models / Services / Requests

- None new or modified. The two filters are optional `GET` parameters read directly off the `Request`.

Controllers

- Added `App\Http\Controllers\Admin\GanttChartController` — `index()` picks the mode from `project_id`, builds the rows (`projectRows()` or `taskRows()`, each honouring its own filters), resolves the axis via `resolveRange()`, then positions everything: `position()` for the bars, `positionMilestones()` for the diamonds, `monthSegments()` for the header blocks and `offsetFor()` for the today line (which returns `null` — and so draws nothing — when the date sits outside the range). `totalDays()` is the single inclusive-day divisor all four share, so no two parts of the chart can measure the axis differently.

Views

- Added `resources/views/admin/gantt-chart/index.blade.php` — a full-page (non-modal) view. A `GET` filter bar whose fields change with the mode (Project + Assignee + Task State when scoped, Project + Project State when not), a Clear link shown only when a filter is active, and the resolved date range shown as a pill. The chart itself is a sticky-left label column beside a scrollable track: month header blocks, a milestone axis row, then one row per bar with dashed month gridlines, the today line, a progress fill and a hover tooltip giving the exact dates and duration. A legend maps every state colour, a footer reports how many bars are plotted, and empty states are handled explicitly (a dashed "no dated tasks to plot" panel rather than an empty frame). All styling lives in a scoped `@push('styles')` block — no shared stylesheet was touched — using Bootstrap CSS variables with literal fallbacks so the chart follows the app's theme, plus a mobile breakpoint that narrows the label column.

- None. The filters submit on change and the chart is static markup, so no script file was needed.

### 2026-08-10 (8)

Completed

- Task Dependencies (ninth Project Management module — a flat predecessor/successor link between two tasks on the same project, with cycle prevention)

Scope decision

- **A flat link table, not embedded on `project_tasks`.** A task can have any number of predecessors and any number of successors, so this is a many-to-many edge list (`task_id` the dependent/successor, `depends_on_task_id` the predecessor), the same structural family as `RfqVendor`'s pivot rather than a column added to Tasks.
- **Both ends must belong to the same project**, enforced in the Form Request naming the problem plainly — a cross-project link would show up on the Gantt Chart or Task Board as a dependency between two unrelated timelines. The create/edit form independently narrows both task dropdowns to a client-side-only "Project" helper select (never submitted), so the UI cannot offer what the validator would reject — the same two-layer approach `ProjectTaskController`'s own milestone-narrowing already established.
- **Real cycle detection, not just a duplicate-pair check.** `(task_id, depends_on_task_id)` is unique at the DB level (named index `ptd_task_depends_unique`), but a cycle of three or more tasks (A depends on B, B depends on C, C depends on A) cannot be expressed as a uniqueness constraint at all — it depends on the shape of the whole graph. `ProjectTaskDependencyRequest::wouldCreateCycle()` walks the existing "depends on" edges starting at the new predecessor and rejects the link if the new successor is reachable, naming both tasks in the message. The traversal excludes the dependency row being edited from its own check, so re-saving an unchanged link never trips over itself. All three shapes verified directly: a two-hop cycle, a same-pair duplicate, and a legitimate third link that shares a predecessor with an existing one.
- **A task cannot depend on itself** (`different:depends_on_task_id`), checked first so the cycle walk never needs to special-case a zero-length loop.
- `dependency_type` covers the four standard project-scheduling links (`finish_to_start`/`start_to_start`/`finish_to_finish`/`start_to_finish`); `lag_days` is signed — positive is a wait after the predecessor, negative is deliberate overlap — capped at ±365 and left nullable/zero when there is none.
- **No change to Tasks, the Task Board or the Gantt Chart.** This module records the links; nothing built in this task makes the Board or the Chart draw them yet — that would be a change to those modules' own controllers and was judged separate, follow-on work rather than something to fold in here silently.

- Added `project_task_dependencies` migration (`database/migrations/2026_08_10_140000_create_project_task_dependencies_table.php`): `task_id`/`depends_on_task_id` both `foreignId` → `project_tasks.id`, `cascadeOnDelete`; `dependency_type` enum (4 values) default `finish_to_start`; `lag_days` integer nullable; `notes` nullable text; `status` boolean default true; named unique index `ptd_task_depends_unique` on `(task_id, depends_on_task_id)`.

- Added `App\Http\Requests\Admin\ProjectTaskDependencyRequest` — `task_id` required `exists:project_tasks,id` plus `different:depends_on_task_id`; `depends_on_task_id` required `exists:project_tasks,id` plus a scoped `Rule::unique('project_task_dependencies','depends_on_task_id')->where(fn ($q) => $q->where('task_id', $this->task_id))->ignore($id)` (the app-level mirror of the DB constraint, giving a friendly message instead of a raw error); `dependency_type` via `Rule::in()`; `lag_days` nullable integer `-365`–`365`; `notes`/`status` standard. `withValidator()` holds the same-project check and the `wouldCreateCycle()` BFS described above.

### 2026-08-11

Completed

- Time Tracking (tenth Project Management module — raw per-employee time logging against a project and optionally a task, with a real start/stop timer alongside manual entry)

Scope decision

- **Deliberately separate from Timesheets, the next roadmap item.** Time Tracking is the raw log — individual entries, each with clock times or a manually-typed duration; Timesheets (not yet built) will presumably be the weekly aggregation-and-approval layer that reads these entries. Keeping the two apart means this module carries no submission/approval workflow of its own (no `entry_status` enum beyond the usual active/inactive `status` toggle) — that lifecycle belongs to Timesheets, not here, the same discipline this sequence has followed throughout (Projects omitted a budget, Milestones omitted a billing amount, Tasks omitted a dependency link).
- **A real start/stop timer, not just a manual-hours form.** This is what makes "Time Tracking" a distinct feature from a weekly timesheet grid. `started_at`/`ended_at` are full datetimes; a row with `started_at` set and `ended_at` still null is a live, running timer (`ProjectTimeEntry::is_running`, computed, not stored — same "derive, never persist a figure that can drift" reasoning as every other computed flag in this project). `hours` is server-computed from the two timestamps whenever both are present, recalculated on every save so a manually-typed figure can never silently disagree with the clock; without a clock-time pair, whatever duration was typed is kept as-is. Verified both paths, including that editing an existing clock-timed entry recomputes `hours` rather than trusting a stale submitted value.
- **Only one running timer per employee, enforced in the service.** `ProjectTimeEntryService::startTimer()` checks for an existing `running()` row for that employee and throws rather than silently abandoning the first timer or letting two run in parallel — verified directly (a second start attempt was rejected with the timer's own explanation).
- **The timer is scoped to the current admin's own linked employee** (`admins.employee_id`, the HRM login-link column added when Employees' "Login" feature was built), not any employee — starting/stopping someone else's timer through this quick action would be acting on their behalf without them present. An admin managing time on behalf of any employee (their own or someone else's, already-finished work) still has the full manual Add/Edit form, which accepts any employee. An admin with no linked employee record sees an honest explanation instead of a broken widget — verified via `startTimerForm()`'s no-employee branch.
- **Either a manual duration or a real clock-time pair, never a bare `started_at`.** The Form Request requires `started_at` and `ended_at` together (`required_with` both ways) and separately requires that at least one of "both clock times" or "a typed `hours` value" be present — so a half-finished clock entry (e.g. a start time with no end) can only exist as a genuine running timer created by `startTimer()`, never hand-typed through the CRUD form. Verified all three shapes: neither present (rejected), only `started_at` (rejected), and a valid hours-only entry (accepted).
- **A task, if chosen, must belong to the selected project** — the same cross-entity guard `ProjectTaskRequest`'s own milestone check and `ProjectTaskDependencyRequest`'s same-project check already established in this sequence, mirrored client-side by narrowing the task dropdown to the selected project on both the manual form and the quick-start form.
- **`employee_id`/`project_id` are both required, `cascadeOnDelete`** — an entry has no meaning without either, the same "required parent-owns-child FK" reasoning as `ProjectTeamMember`'s own employee/project pair; `project_task_id` is optional, `nullOnDelete`, since time can be logged against a project generally. Verified the employee-delete cascade directly.
- **The "My Timer" widget is server-rendered, not part of the DataTable** — a running timer belongs to the page header, always visible regardless of what the list below is filtered to, so starting/stopping it triggers a full page reload (a small, deliberate deviation from every other module's `dataTableInstance.ajax.reload()`-only pattern, since that call alone would leave a just-started timer invisible until the next full navigation) rather than the standard `.ajax-form` handler.

Database

- Added `project_time_entries` migration (`database/migrations/2026_08_11_090000_create_project_time_entries_table.php`): `employee_id`/`project_id` both `foreignId`, `cascadeOnDelete`; `project_task_id` nullable `foreignId` → `project_tasks.id`, `nullOnDelete`; `work_date` required date; `started_at`/`ended_at` nullable datetimes; `hours` decimal(6,2) nullable, server-computed when both timestamps are present; `is_billable` boolean default true; `description` nullable text; `status` boolean default true.

Models

- Added `App\Models\ProjectTimeEntry` — casts the three date/datetime fields, `hours` to `decimal:2`, `is_billable`/`status` to boolean; accessors `is_running` and `elapsed_minutes` (the latter only meaningful while running, a live figure never cached); relations `employee()`, `project()`, `task()` (→ `ProjectTask` via `project_task_id`); `scopeActive()` and the new `scopeRunning()` (`whereNotNull('started_at')->whereNull('ended_at')`), used by both the service's one-timer-per-employee guard and the index's "Running Only" filter so the two can never disagree about what counts as running.

Services

- Added `App\Services\ProjectTimeEntryService` — `create()`/`update()` both route through `withComputedHours()` (the clock-times-take-precedence logic described above); `startTimer()` and `stopTimer()` are the two new timer-lifecycle methods, each throwing a plain `RuntimeException` on misuse (already-running / not-running) rather than silently no-op'ing, consistent with the plain-exception convention this project has used since the Workflow Engine's own `WorkflowEngineService`; `delete()` is a plain model delete.

Requests

- Added `App\Http\Requests\Admin\ProjectTimeEntryRequest` — `employee_id`/`project_id` required `exists:` checks; `project_task_id` nullable `exists:project_tasks,id`; `work_date` required date; `started_at`/`ended_at` both `required_with` each other, `ended_at` additionally `after:started_at`; `hours` nullable numeric `0.01`–`24`; `is_billable`/`description`/`status` standard. `withValidator()` holds the "clock pair or hours, not neither" check and the same-project task check described above.

Controllers

- Added `App\Http\Controllers\Admin\ProjectTimeEntryController` — standard CRUD, module string `project-time-entries`, plus three new actions beyond the usual seven: `startTimerForm()`/`startTimer()`/`stopTimer()`. Index eager-loads `employee`/`project.client`/`task`; adds `project_id`, `employee_id`, a tri-state `billable` filter (guarded against `null`/`''` so `0` — non-billable — is a real filter value, the same guard `FollowUpController`'s `is_completed` filter already established) and a `running` filter (via the new `scopeRunning()`); search matches the description or either the project's or employee's name/code; sorted `work_date DESC` (a log, not a worklist, same ordering choice as Maintenance History). `duration_col` renders a live "Running" badge with elapsed time for an in-progress entry, the clock-time range for a finished one, or the plain typed hours for a manual entry — three states in one column. `currentEmployeeId()` resolves `auth()->guard('admin')->user()?->employee_id` once, shared by the index's widget data and both timer actions.

- Added `public/assets/system/js/pages/project-time-entries.js` — the usual DataTable init/search/pagination/status-filter boilerplate, `filterTimeEntryTaskOptions()` (the same project-narrows-task technique as `project-tasks.js`'s milestone filter, shared by both the manual form and the quick-start form via a project/task class-name pair), a light `bindTimeEntryDurationToggle()` UX nudge that clears the hours field when a clock time is typed and vice versa, and the two new pieces: a plain (non-`.ajax-form`) submit handler for `.start-timer-form` and a `.time-entry-stop-btn` click handler, both reloading the page on success for the reason above rather than only redrawing the DataTable. `tickMyTimerElapsed()` ticks the widget's elapsed-time readout client-side every 30 seconds — a display convenience only; the authoritative hours figure is always computed server-side when the timer actually stops.

### 2026-08-12

Completed

- Timesheets (eleventh Project Management module — weekly grouping, submission and approval of an employee's Time Tracking entries; plus a small, documented retrofit onto Time Tracking itself for entry-locking)

Scope decision

- **A grouping-and-workflow layer over Time Tracking, not a second place to log hours.** Time Tracking's own changelog entry explicitly deferred "the weekly aggregation-and-approval layer" to this module — this is that layer. A `ProjectTimesheet` header never carries its own hand-typed hours; `total_hours`/`billable_hours` are always summed from whichever `ProjectTimeEntry` rows are linked to it.
- **The link is a retrofitted FK on Time Entries, not a join table.** Followed the "build the dependency, then retrofit" pattern used repeatedly in this project (Customer Groups → `customers.customer_group_id`, Sales Targets → `sales_orders.assigned_to`): a follow-up migration adds `project_time_entries.project_timesheet_id`, nullable and `nullOnDelete` — an entry is a valid standalone record before it's ever grouped into a week, and survives if its timesheet is later deleted. One `ProjectTimeEntry` can only ever belong to one `ProjectTimesheet`, which a join table would not have expressed as directly.
- **"Generate", not "Create".** The create form only asks for an employee and any date inside the target week; `ProjectTimesheetService::generate()` normalizes that to the Monday–Sunday range (`Carbon::startOfWeek(MONDAY)`/`endOfWeek(SUNDAY)`), finds-or-creates the header via `firstOrNew(['employee_id', 'week_start_date'])` (the same tuple the table's own unique index enforces), and links every matching, currently-unlinked-or-already-linked entry onto it — safe to call again later ("Regenerate") to pull in entries added or corrected after the fact. Verified directly that calling it twice for the same week returns the same header with the same totals rather than creating a duplicate.
- **A still-running timer is deliberately excluded from generation.** `generate()`'s entry query adds `whereNull('started_at')->orWhereNotNull('ended_at')` — a timer with no end time yet has no real hours to summarize, so it is left out until it's stopped and the timesheet is regenerated. This was caught and fixed while writing the service, before any test ran: without the filter, a mid-shift timer pulled into a timesheet would either contribute `null`/zero hours today and silently disappear from the total once stopped, or worse, get locked mid-run once the timesheet was submitted. Verified directly: a running entry logged inside the target week stayed unlinked after `generate()`.
- **Regeneration is only possible while `draft` or `rejected`** — once `submitted` or `approved`, `generate()` throws rather than silently re-summing a period that's already under review or signed off. This is the same guard, expressed the same way, as the `is_locked` check described below; both read `ProjectTimesheet::LOCKED_STATUSES` so the two can never disagree about what counts as "already committed."
- **New cross-module consistency rule, the centerpiece of this task**: once a timesheet is `submitted`, every `ProjectTimeEntry` linked to it becomes locked (`ProjectTimeEntry::is_locked`, a computed accessor — not stored, so it can never drift from its timesheet's actual state) and `ProjectTimeEntryService::update()`/`delete()` now both reject any attempt to touch a locked entry with a plain `RuntimeException`, regardless of which screen the edit is attempted from. This is the same category of retrofit `AssetAssignmentService` made to `Asset.asset_status` and `PaymentReceiveService` made to `SalesInvoice.amount_paid` — a small, necessary change to an already-shipped module, made because the new module's core guarantee (a submitted week's hours are exactly what gets reviewed) cannot be enforced any other way. Time Tracking's own list/action views were updated to show a lock badge and hide the Edit/Delete buttons on a locked row, so the UI reflects the same rule the service enforces — verified both the service-level rejection and, separately, that rejecting the timesheet unlocks its entries again (confirmed by successfully editing a previously-locked entry immediately after rejection).
- **Rejecting, not deleting.** A `submitted` timesheet can be `rejected` with a required reason (kept as a plain `RuntimeException`-free three-line service method, not a workflow-engine integration — this is a single yes/no gate, not a multi-step approval chain, so reaching for the existing generic Workflow Engine here would have been over-engineering for what it actually needs). Rejecting unlocks its entries and clears `rejection_reason` on the next successful `generate()`, so an old rejection message can never linger after the week has been corrected and resubmitted. `approved_by`/`approved_at` are stamped on approval and never touched again — an approved timesheet is a closed historical record, the same "snapshot, not live" reasoning `SalesCommission` already established, distinct from `SalesTarget`'s live-computed figures.
- **The plain edit form only ever touches `notes` and the archive `status` toggle** — a second, narrower `ProjectTimesheetUpdateRequest` alongside the one used by the "Generate" form, since the two forms validate almost entirely different things (one submits `employee_id`+a date, the other submits neither). Dates, hours and the workflow state are exclusively managed through `generate()`/`submit()`/`approve()`/`reject()`, never through a hand-edited field — verified that `total_hours`, `week_start_date`, etc. are genuinely absent from the update Request's rules.

### 2026-08-13

Completed

- Project Expenses (twelfth Project Management module — costs incurred against a project, with a lightweight pending/approved/rejected review, the input Project Billing and Project Profitability Reports will read)

Scope decision

- **Its own table, deliberately not HRM's `expense_claims`.** Checked the Naming/Table Conflict Guard and `ExpenseClaim` directly before starting: `expense_claims` is an employee's personal reimbursement claim, `Approvable` and wired into the generic Workflow Engine. A project expense is a different thing — a project-scoped cost record that may or may not involve any employee at all (a vendor invoice, a flat recurring charge). `project_expenses` is its own table; an employee attributed here as "incurred by" is attribution only, not a reimbursement — someone wanting money back for an out-of-pocket project cost still files a normal HRM Expense Claim. This is stated explicitly in the migration and on the create form's footnote, so the missing reimbursement machinery reads as deliberate rather than an oversight.
- **`expense_category` reuses the exact 7-value set `ProjectBudgetItem::CATEGORIES` already established** (`labour`/`materials`/`equipment`/`subcontract`/`travel`/`software`/`other`) — defined as `ProjectExpense`'s own constant rather than importing the other model's, per this project's standing "each model owns its own enum constant even when the value set is conceptually shared" convention (`SalesOrder::STATUSES` vs `SalesQuotation::STATUSES` is the precedent). The shared vocabulary is deliberate: Project Profitability Reports (a later roadmap item) will presumably want to compare actual spend by category against the budget's own category breakdown, and mismatched category vocabularies between the two tables would make that comparison meaningless.
- **A plain pending/approved/rejected gate, not a Workflow Engine integration.** `ExpenseClaim` itself implements `Approvable` for the generic multi-step Workflow Engine, but that machinery exists for genuinely multi-step, configurable approval chains — this is a single yes/no review gate, the same complexity class as `AssetDisposal`'s or `BankReconciliation`'s own plain-service approval methods. Reaching for the Workflow Engine here would have been over-engineering for what the checklist item actually needs; if a real multi-step approval chain is ever requested for project costs, wiring it in later is exactly the kind of additive change this project's HRM/Purchase modules already demonstrate is straightforward.
- **Edit is locked once approved; delete is not.** `ProjectExpenseService::guardNotApproved()` rejects `update()` on an approved record with a plain `RuntimeException` (an approved expense may already be reflected in a client bill or a profitability figure — editing it afterward would let those numbers silently disagree with what was actually approved), but `delete()` is left unguarded so an admin can still remove an approved record outright as a deliberate corrective action. This is the same edit-locked-but-deletable shape `SalesCommission` uses after a commission is marked paid. The list mirrors the same rule in the UI — an approved row shows a lock icon in place of the Edit button, Delete stays available — rather than disabling form fields, which was tried first and reverted (see Notes).
- **`reject()` clears `approved_by`/`approved_at`** even though only a `pending` record can be rejected in the first place (so those fields are always already null when reject fires) — included anyway as a defensive no-op, cheap insurance against a future code path that might call `reject()` from a different state.
- **A real file-upload receipt, mirroring `ExpenseClaimService`'s exact pattern** (`store('receipts/project-expenses', 'public')`, same MIME whitelist `pdf,jpg,jpeg,png`, same `deleteFile()`-before-`storeFile()` replace-on-update sequence, same physical-file cleanup on delete) — reused rather than reinvented, since the two file-upload shapes are otherwise identical.
- **A real bug was caught and fixed during verification, not left in place**: `ProjectExpense::create()` initially relied on the `approval_status` column's DB-level `default('pending')` rather than setting it explicitly in the service. Eloquent's `create()` does not re-query the row afterward, so the in-memory model returned to the controller reported a **blank** `approval_status` immediately after creation — which would have shown up wrong in that same request's JSON response and activity-log entry, and caused the very first `reject()` call in testing to fail for the wrong reason (the guard correctly saw a non-`'pending'` value, just the wrong one). Fixed by having `ProjectExpenseService::create()` set `'approval_status' => $data['approval_status'] ?? 'pending'` explicitly before the insert, the same "don't rely on a DB default the in-memory model won't see" lesson this project has now hit more than once. Re-verified after the fix: a freshly created expense correctly reports `approval_status === 'pending'` immediately, with no query needed in between.

### 2026-08-14

Completed

- Project Billing (thirteenth Project Management module — a project's own client-billing document, drawing its lines from billable Time Entries and approved Project Expenses; plus small, documented retrofits onto both to prevent double-billing)

Scope decision

- **Its own document, deliberately not a Sales Invoice.** Checked the Naming/Table Conflict Guard and `SalesInvoice` directly before starting: Sales Invoices bill a customer against product-based Sales Orders; this bills a project's client for service-based work (time and expenses). `project_invoices`/`project_invoice_items` are their own tables — a genuinely different billing flow, not a variant of the Sales one.
- **No retrofitted "billed" column on Time Entries or Expenses — billed status is derived, not stored.** The obvious design (mirroring Timesheets' own `project_timesheet_id` retrofit) would have added `project_invoice_id` directly onto both `project_time_entries` and `project_expenses`. Instead, each invoice line (`ProjectInvoiceItem`) already carries its own `project_time_entry_id`/`project_expense_id`, and an inverse `HasOne` relation (`ProjectTimeEntry::invoiceItem()` / `ProjectExpense::invoiceItem()`) is all that's needed to answer "has this been billed, and is that bill still active?" — checking whether the linked item's invoice has `invoice_status !== 'cancelled'`. This avoids a second schema retrofit entirely and, as a direct consequence, **cancelling an invoice automatically frees every source it had billed with no separate unlink step anywhere** — there is no stored flag to reset, since "billed" was never anything but a live query in the first place. Verified directly: a time entry billed on a since-cancelled invoice correctly reported `is_locked = false` again with no code path that explicitly cleared anything.
- **Double-billing the same entry or expense is blocked in three independent layers**, each a genuine, verified guard rather than decorative redundancy: a named DB unique index on each of `project_invoice_items.project_time_entry_id`/`project_expense_id` (defense of last resort); the picker itself excludes anything already billed on a non-cancelled invoice (`ProjectInvoiceController::formData()`); and the Form Request re-checks the same condition server-side with a friendly message naming the problem, since a stale picker (two admins working at once) could otherwise slip past the client-side exclusion. Verified: attempting to bill an already-billed time entry on a second invoice was rejected with "That time entry has already been billed on another invoice."
- **A cross-project guard, the same pattern `ProjectTaskRequest`'s milestone check and `ProjectTaskDependencyRequest`'s same-project check already established in this sequence**: a line's time entry or expense must belong to the invoice's own `project_id`, checked in the Form Request and mirrored client-side by narrowing the picker to the header's selected project. Verified: a time entry from a different project was rejected by name.
- **Payment is a single running total on the invoice itself, not a second Payment-Receive-style allocation ledger.** Sales' own Payment Receive module exists for exactly that shape against Sales Invoices; building a parallel allocation table here for one checklist item would have been over-engineering. `recordPayment()` is a plain guarded method (must be `sent`/`partially_paid`; amount must be positive and not exceed the remaining balance) that derives `invoice_status` fresh from the new `amount_paid` on every call, so the status can never drift from what's actually been paid.
- **Cancelling, not deleting, is the normal way to void a mistaken bill** — a `paid` invoice cannot be cancelled (undo that with a real correction elsewhere, not by erasing the fact that money changed hands), but `draft`/`sent`/`partially_paid` all can be. `delete()` itself carries no status guard at all — an admin can always remove an invoice outright as a deliberate corrective action, the same edit-locked-but-deletable shape `SalesCommission`/`ProjectExpense` already use in this project — but `update()` is guarded against `paid`/`cancelled` (a closed document shouldn't have its lines silently rewritten).
- **A genuinely new class of bug was caught and fixed during verification, not left in place**: `ProjectTimeEntryService::guardNotLocked()`'s error message was written back when the only lock reason was a submitted timesheet, and hardcoded that wording. Once this task extended `ProjectTimeEntry::is_locked` to also cover being billed on a live invoice, that same hardcoded message became actively wrong for the new case — editing a *billed* (not timesheeted) entry correctly threw, but told the admin it was "part of a submitted timesheet," which was false and would have sent them looking in the wrong place. Fixed by having the guard check which of the two independent lock reasons actually applies and naming that one specifically. Caught by this task's own lifecycle test, not left for a user to discover — re-verified afterward that a billed-but-not-timesheeted entry now correctly reports "already been billed to the client," and a timesheet-locked one still reports the original message.
- **`ProjectExpenseService::guardNotApproved()` was renamed to `guardEditable()` and extended with a second, independent check** (`ProjectExpense::is_invoiced`, the same inverse-relation technique as the time-entry side) — an expense can now be edit-locked for either reason, each with its own message, mirroring the time-entry side exactly rather than inventing a different shape for what is structurally the same problem.

- Added `project_invoices`/`project_invoice_items` in one migration (`database/migrations/2026_08_14_090000_create_project_invoices_table.php`):

  - `project_invoice_items`: `project_invoice_id` `cascadeOnDelete`; `source_type` enum (`time_entry`/`expense`/`manual`) default `manual`; `project_time_entry_id`/`project_expense_id` both nullable `foreignId`s, `nullOnDelete` (a line traced to a real source keeps its own billed figures even if that source row is later removed; only a manual line has neither set); `description`/`quantity`/`unit_price`/`line_total` (the last server-computed); named unique indexes `pii_time_entry_unique`/`pii_expense_unique` on the two source columns (defense-in-depth against double-billing, per the Scope decision above).

### 2026-08-15

Completed — **Project Management module is now fully complete (14/14 roadmap features)**

- Project Profitability Reports (fourteenth and final Project Management module — revenue billed, cost incurred, budget vs. actual, and a resulting profit/margin per project)

Scope decision

- Same "controller only, no new table/Model/Service/Request" shape as every closing report in this project (Financial Reports, Sales Reports, Purchase Reports, Inventory Reports, Asset Reports) — a single `GET` route, one controller `index()`, one Blade view, computing its own aggregation independently rather than sharing a service with the modules it reads from.
- **Revenue is every non-cancelled `ProjectInvoice.grand_total` for the project** — the same "exclude cancelled" convention every prior Sales/Purchase/Accounting report already follows. `balance_due` is an accessor, not a column, so outstanding amounts are summed in PHP, the same constraint Accounts Receivable/Payable and Sales/Purchase Reports already work around identically.
- **Cost is every `approval_status = 'approved'` Project Expense's `amount`, regardless of `is_billable`.** A cost is real to the project whether or not the client is being charged for it; `is_billable` only governs whether it can be billed on a Project Invoice (`ProjectExpense::scopeBillableApproved()`, reused here for a separate "recoverable cost" figure), not whether it happened.
- **Time Tracking is deliberately NOT folded into the cost figure — checked, not assumed.** `ProjectTimeEntry`'s migration and model were inspected directly and carry no hourly rate anywhere, and no rate exists on `Employee` or any HRM payroll table either. Inventing a rate to price labour hours would misrepresent cost with a fabricated number, so the report instead shows hours logged (total and billable) as its own informational figure, explicitly labelled and called out with a footnote stating it is excluded from the profit/loss math. If a billing rate is ever added to Time Tracking, folding labour cost in here becomes a natural follow-up, not something invented speculatively now.
- **"The budget" for a project is its highest-`version` active `ProjectBudget` row, regardless of `budget_status`.** Project Budgets is explicitly versioned (draft → approved → revised → closed) per project, and the most recently numbered version is the one that currently represents "what was planned" — the same way an edited document's latest state is what matters, not its approval history. Verified directly: a project with a draft v1 (1,000) and an approved v2 (4,500) correctly reported the v2 total as current, not v1's. A project with no budget at all is reported as unbudgeted (`budget_total = null`) rather than assumed to be zero.
- **Budget-vs-actual by category compares `project_budget_items` against approved `project_expenses` grouped by `expense_category`** — the two tables deliberately share the same 7-value category enum (documented in Project Expenses' own changelog entry specifically so this comparison would be meaningful), so no category-name mapping was needed. Every category present on either side is shown, including a budget line with no matching spend yet (shows actual 0) and an expense category the budget never planned for (shows budgeted 0) — verified both directions in the same test.
- Two modes on one page, the shape General Ledger established and every drill-down report since reuses: no project selected shows every active project's profitability ranked by profit descending, plus org-wide totals; selecting one project shows its full detail (headline stats, budget-vs-actual table with a budget-used progress bar, hours logged). The overview's project name links through to its own detail view; the detail view's "Open Project" link uses the established `?search=<code>` convention (the same technique the Task Board's card shortcut and Gantt Chart use to open a specific record in a list view) rather than linking directly to a modal-only edit route.

### 2026-08-17

Completed

- Ticket Creation (second Support module — the module's primary entity: a support ticket, optionally linked to an existing Sales customer or HRM employee, or a free-text requester)

Scope decision

- **Deliberately minimal** — the same discipline followed throughout this project for a module's primary entity (Asset Register carried no purchase/assignment/location fields; Projects carried no budget figure). Ticket Assignment, Ticket Status, Priority Management, SLA Management and Escalation Rules are all separate, not-yet-built roadmap items immediately after this one; none of that logic was built speculatively here.
- **`priority`/`ticket_status` are fixed enums, not configurable masters** — the same "hardcoded enum now, retrofit a configurable master + optional FK only on a real need" choice already made for Chart of Accounts' `account_type` ahead of Account Types. Ticket Status and Priority Management, both later roadmap items, will presumably layer their own configurable masters on top of these exactly the way Account Types layered onto Chart of Accounts — not built now.
- **`ticket_category_id` is nullable at the DB level with `nullOnDelete`, but required in the Form Request** — the identical deliberate split Asset Register uses for `asset_category_id`: no ticket may be filed without a category, but deleting a category must not take the ticket register with it. Verified directly: deleting a category left its ticket intact with `ticket_category_id = NULL`.
- **Two independent, optional requester links, not a false choice** — `customer_id` (Sales' existing `customers` table) and `raised_by_employee_id` (HRM's existing `employees` table), plus free-text `requester_name`/`requester_email`/`requester_phone` for a ticket raised by neither (an ad hoc walk-in, or later a Customer Portal submission with no linked record yet). The same "two optional responsible parties" reasoning already used for Asset Maintenance Schedule's `vendor_id`/`assigned_to` pair. A computed `requester_label` accessor resolves to whichever of the three actually applies, checked in that order, so the list/detail views never need to repeat the fallback logic themselves.
- **The service owns completion consistency for both `resolved_at` and `closed_at`**, the same pattern Project/Milestone/Task/Asset Disposal already established: marking a ticket Resolved or Closed stamps the matching timestamp (now, if none given); moving it back off either clears that timestamp. A ticket closed directly (skipping Resolved) has its `resolved_at` backfilled to the same moment, since a closed ticket is, by definition, no longer open.
- **A real bug was caught and fixed during this task's own verification, not left in place**: the first implementation cleared `resolved_at`/`closed_at` by checking the ticket's *previous* `ticket_status` value (`elseif ($ticket->ticket_status === 'resolved')`) — which missed the case where a ticket went `resolved → closed → open`, since its status immediately before reopening was `closed`, not `resolved`, even though `resolved_at` was still populated from the earlier transition. Fixed by checking whether the timestamp column itself is actually set (`elseif ($ticket->resolved_at)`) rather than inferring it from the status history. Caught by this module's own tinker test (which walks exactly that three-step transition) before the module was reported complete, then re-verified clean.
- `ticket_number` is server-generated (`TKT-`) and stripped on update, since any future Ticket Assignment/SLA/Escalation record will reference it — verified an injected `ticket_number` of "HACKED" was ignored.

### 2026-08-18

Completed

- Ticket Assignment (third Support module — a history table of who is handling each ticket, with reassignment tracked over time)

Scope decision

- **A history table, not a single "current agent" column on tickets** — every handover kept as its own row, so a ticket's assignment history survives the next reassignment. The same structural family as `AssetAssignment` (one active row at a time, closed out before a new one is opened), adapted here for "who is handling this ticket" instead of "who is holding this asset".
- **The agent is a system login (`Admin`), not an HRM `Employee`** — the same actor entity every other reviewer/approver FK in this project uses (`approved_by`, `created_by`, `cashier_id`, ...), since handling a ticket is done by whoever is logged in to the ERP, not necessarily someone tracked in the HR module the way a physical asset's holder is. Both `ticket_id` and `assigned_to` are required, `cascadeOnDelete` — an assignment record has no meaning without either side of it, the same "required parent-owns-child FK" reasoning `AssetAssignment` already established for its own asset/employee pair; verified directly in both directions.
- **`assignment_status` is `assigned`/`reassigned`/`cancelled`, not `assigned`/`returned`/`cancelled`** — a ticket doesn't get "returned" the way a physical asset does, but the shape is otherwise identical: one open ("assigned") row per ticket at a time, closed out by marking it `reassigned` (moved to someone else) or `cancelled` (removed with no successor) before a new active assignment can be created. The one-active-assignment-per-ticket rule is enforced the same way Asset Assignment enforces its own — in the Form Request, not the schema, since it depends on the enum value of *other* rows. Verified directly: a second `assigned` row for the same ticket was rejected naming the ticket number, and creating a new one after marking the first `reassigned` succeeded cleanly.
- **Deliberately does NOT touch `tickets.ticket_status`** — unlike `AssetAssignmentService`, which keeps `assets.asset_status` truthful as custody changes, this service has no side effect on the ticket at all. A ticket's work-progress state is a separate concern owned by the Tickets screen itself, and "Ticket Status" is its own, not-yet-built roadmap item; auto-driving `ticket_status` from assignment activity here would either duplicate or pre-empt that future module's job. Verified directly: assigning and reassigning a ticket left its `ticket_status` completely unchanged.
- **Closed tickets are excluded from the create picker, but a closed ticket's own existing assignment is not lost on edit** — the same "exclude, but never orphan the current selection" picker technique `AssetAssignmentController`/`AssetPurchaseController` already established. Verified both halves: a closed ticket was absent from the create dropdown, but present when editing its own already-existing assignment.

### 2026-08-19

Completed

- Ticket Status (fourth Support module — a configurable, finer-grained status master layered on top of Tickets' fixed `ticket_status` enum, plus a small, documented retrofit onto Ticket Creation)

Scope decision

- **Layers on top of the fixed enum, does not replace it** — the exact same "hardcoded enum now, retrofit a configurable master + optional FK only on a real need" pattern Account Types already built on top of Chart of Accounts' `account_type` enum, predicted explicitly in Ticket Creation's own changelog entry. `tickets.ticket_status` stays the always-present, universal lifecycle bucket (`open`/`in_progress`/`on_hold`/`resolved`/`closed`) every other part of the Tickets module (`is_overdue`, `scopeOpen()`, the resolved/closed timestamp logic) already keys off; `ticket_statuses` lets an admin define named sub-statuses (e.g. "Waiting on Customer", "Escalated") that each declare which of those five fixed buckets they count as via `maps_to`.
- **`maps_to` is the "nature" equivalent** — the same cross-classification field `AccountType.nature` plays against `ChartOfAccount.account_type`. Enforced with the identical technique: `TicketRequest::withValidator()` gained a second closure rejecting a ticket whose custom `ticket_status_id` maps to a different bucket than its own submitted `ticket_status`, naming both values in the message. Verified directly: a `ticket_status = open` ticket paired with a custom status mapping to `on_hold` was rejected; the same pairing with `ticket_status = on_hold` was accepted.
- **`is_terminal` is a computed accessor, not a stored column** — a custom status is terminal exactly when the fixed bucket it maps to is one `Ticket::CLOSED_STATUSES` already treats as closed, so a second stored flag could only ever drift from that. Verified both values: a status mapping to `on_hold` correctly reports `false`, one mapping to `closed` correctly reports `true`.
- **`ticket_status_id` is nullable, `nullOnDelete`, added via a follow-up migration** — not an edit to the original `tickets` migration, the same "build the dependency, then retrofit the FK" pattern used repeatedly in this project. A ticket can exist with no custom status at all (it always has its fixed enum), and deleting a custom status must not delete the tickets carrying it. Verified directly: deleting a custom status left its ticket intact with `ticket_status_id = NULL` and its own `ticket_status` completely unaffected.
- **The custom status is shown as an additional line under the existing fixed-enum badge in the Tickets list, not in place of it** — the same additive display Chart of Accounts uses for its own optional Account Type badge, so nothing about the already-shipped `ticket_status_badge` column's meaning changed, it just gained an optional second line.
- **The create/edit forms narrow the Custom Status dropdown client-side to only the options whose `maps_to` matches the currently-selected Ticket State**, clearing the selection if it no longer applies — mirroring the server-side cross-consistency rule so the form rarely trips it, the same "narrow the picker, don't just reject after the fact" technique used throughout this project (e.g. `ProjectTaskController`'s milestone-narrowing).
- `color` (a plain hex string) and `sort_order` were added to the master since a configurable status genuinely benefits from a distinct display colour and a defined ordering (the same two fields `WorkflowStatus` already carries for exactly this purpose) — no other module retrofit was needed for either.

- Added a follow-up migration (`database/migrations/2026_08_19_090001_add_ticket_status_id_to_tickets_table.php`) adding `tickets.ticket_status_id`, nullable `foreignId` → `ticket_statuses.id`, `nullOnDelete`, positioned `->after('ticket_status')`.

### 2026-08-21

Completed

- SLA Management (sixth Support module — response/resolution time targets per fixed priority, automatically applied to tickets with breach tracking, plus a small, documented retrofit onto Ticket Creation)

Scope decision

- **A genuinely new feature, not another "configurable master on a fixed enum" like Ticket Status/Priority Management** — this module computes and tracks real due-date targets against tickets, not just a finer-grained classification label.
- **One `SlaPolicy` per fixed priority bucket, enforced with a real DB unique constraint on `priority`** (plus the app-level mirror in the Form Request for a friendly message) — a ticket's applicable policy is always an unambiguous single lookup, never a pick between several candidates for the same priority. Deliberately keyed off the always-present fixed `priority` enum, not the optional, admin-configurable `TicketPriority` — the same "fixed enum drives the core logic, the optional custom layer stays independent" separation `ticket_status_id`/`ticket_priority_id` both already maintain.
- **`sla_policy_id` on tickets is purely for traceability/audit — never user-selectable.** Unlike Ticket Status/Priority (where the admin explicitly picks an optional custom classification), the SLA policy is fully auto-resolved from the ticket's own fixed `priority`; no dropdown was added to the Ticket form for it.
- **Due-date targets are recomputed fresh on every ticket save, not locked forever at creation** — a deliberate, explicit departure from this project's usual "stored financial snapshot" precedent (e.g. `AssetDisposal.book_value_at_disposal`). That precedent exists because those figures represent a completed financial event with no versioning concept behind it worth re-deriving. SLA policies, by contrast, are a plain, in-place-edited master (no policy-versioning/history anywhere in this project), so "the current target" is the only meaningful answer available — the same reasoning was written directly into `TicketService::withSlaFields()`'s own doc comment. If a ticket's priority changes, or the matching policy's hours are edited before the ticket is next saved, its deadlines update accordingly; this is treated as the more useful behaviour for an *operational* SLA rather than a risk to guard against.
- **Both due dates are anchored on the ticket's own `created_at`, not "now" at save time** — a ticket created three days ago and only just re-saved should show its resolution target as three days closer to being breached, not freshly reset. For `create()`, where the ticket doesn't exist yet, `Carbon::now()` stands in as a close approximation of the imminent `created_at`.
- **`first_responded_at` is a plain fact, stamped once by a dedicated "Record First Response" quick action, never recomputed by the normal save path** — there is no ticket-reply/comment feature anywhere in this project to observe a real response event from, so a manual, guarded stamp (rejecting a second attempt, the same "quick action guards its own state transition" pattern `ProjectInvoiceService::markSent()` uses) is the honest alternative to inventing one. A ticket that reaches `resolved`/`closed` with `first_responded_at` still unset is backfilled to the same moment — the same "can't reach a later state without implicitly passing through an earlier one" logic already used for `resolved_at`/`closed_at` themselves.
- **Two live breach accessors (`is_response_breached`, `is_resolution_breached`), computed, not stored** — the same reasoning behind every other `is_overdue`-style accessor in this project (a stored flag would need a scheduled job to become true as a deadline passes). Both are suppressed once the ticket is closed, mirroring `is_overdue`'s own closed-state suppression — this module is scoped as a live operational alert, not a historical compliance report (that would be a natural fit for the future Support Reports module, not invented here).
- **`nullOnDelete` on `sla_policy_id` deliberately does *not* clear the two due-date columns** — verified directly: deleting the governing policy leaves the ticket's `sla_policy_id` null but its `first_response_due_at`/`resolution_due_at` untouched, since those already-computed values remain valid historical facts about what was targeted, independent of whether the policy record used to compute them still exists.

Database

- Added `sla_policies` migration (`database/migrations/2026_08_21_090000_create_sla_policies_table.php`): `name` unique required; `priority` enum (`low`/`medium`/`high`/`urgent`) **unique**; `response_time_hours`/`resolution_time_hours` both `decimal(6,2)` required; `description` nullable text; `status` boolean default true.
- Added a follow-up migration (`database/migrations/2026_08_21_090001_add_sla_fields_to_tickets_table.php`) adding four columns to `tickets`, all nullable: `sla_policy_id` (`foreignId` → `sla_policies.id`, `nullOnDelete`), `first_response_due_at`, `resolution_due_at`, `first_responded_at` (all `dateTime`).

Models

- Added `App\Models\SlaPolicy` — `public const PRIORITIES`; casts both hour fields to `decimal:2`, `status` to boolean; accessor `priority_label`; relation `tickets(): HasMany`; `scopeActive()`.
- Updated `App\Models\Ticket` — added `sla_policy_id`/`first_response_due_at`/`resolution_due_at`/`first_responded_at` to `$fillable` and their `datetime` casts; added `slaPolicy(): BelongsTo`; added `getIsResponseBreachedAttribute()`/`getIsResolutionBreachedAttribute()` (both described above).

Services

- Added `App\Services\SlaPolicyService` — plain `create()`/`update()`/`delete()`, the same minimal shape as `TicketStatusService`/`TicketPriorityService`.
- Updated `App\Services\TicketService` — added `recordFirstResponse()` (the guarded quick action described above); `withDerivedFields()` now also backfills `first_responded_at` on a direct-to-closed transition and delegates to the new `withSlaFields()`, which resolves the applicable `SlaPolicy` by the ticket's fixed `priority` and (re)computes both due dates anchored on `created_at` — both new methods documented in full above.

Requests

Index `withCount('tickets')`, adds a `priority` filter; sorted via `orderByRaw("FIELD(priority, 'urgent','high','medium','low')")` since there are only ever up to 4 rows and this reads as a natural escalation ladder, with the JS `order: []` so DataTables never appends a competing client-side order. ### 2026-08-22

Completed

- Escalation Rules (seventh Support module — what to do when a ticket breaches its SLA, building directly on the breach detection SLA Management just shipped)

Scope decision

- **A natural continuation of SLA Management, not a fresh concept** — escalation triggers off the exact `is_response_breached`/`is_resolution_breached` accessors that module already computes, so this checklist item adds "then what" on top of the "is this late" SLA Management already answered, rather than inventing a second, parallel notion of lateness (e.g. a raw "hours since created" timer).
- **Two real tables**: `escalation_rules` (the configurable master an admin edits — one rule per `(priority, trigger)` combination, enforced with a real composite unique DB index, the same "exactly one unambiguous lookup" reasoning `SlaPolicy`'s own single-column unique on `priority` established, just spanning two columns here since both narrow the match) and `ticket_escalations` (a system-generated history log of every time a ticket was actually escalated — the same "real persisted history, not just an activity-log line" reasoning `TicketAssignment` already established for its own table).
- **Deliberately a manual, admin-triggered quick action — never an automatic background sweep.** Nothing in this project runs a scheduled "check every open ticket" job; building one here would be a different, much larger feature (a real job-scheduler/queue concern) than this checklist item calls for. An "Escalate" button appears on a ticket only once it has actually breached and is not already closed; clicking it looks up and applies whatever rule matches.
- **Resolution breach takes precedence over response breach** when a ticket has somehow breached both at once — the more severe of the two conditions is what gets acted on, a single deterministic choice rather than an ambiguous "which one" prompt.
- **Two independent, optional actions per rule** — reassign to a specific agent, bump the priority, or both — mirroring the "two optional responsible parties, not a false choice" reasoning already used for Asset Maintenance Schedule's `vendor_id`/`assigned_to` pair. The Form Request rejects a rule with *neither* action set, since a no-op escalation rule would be silently useless.
- **Reassignment bypasses `TicketAssignmentService`/`TicketAssignmentRequest` and manually closes the existing active assignment first** — a deliberate, documented necessity, not an oversight: `TicketAssignmentService::create()` is a plain pass-through with no validation of its own (the one-active-assignment-per-ticket rule lives entirely in `TicketAssignmentRequest`, which this internal call never goes through), so `TicketEscalationService` explicitly marks any existing `assigned` row `reassigned` before opening a new one — the same close-then-create sequence a human using the Ticket Assignment screen would otherwise have to perform by hand. Verified directly: escalating a ticket already assigned to one agent correctly closed that assignment and left exactly one active assignment, now on the new agent.
- **A priority bump routes through a new, small, dedicated `TicketService::changePriority()` method**, not a full `update()` call — the same "dedicated method for one specific transition" pattern `OpportunityService::updateStage()` already established, avoiding the need to assemble a complete `TicketRequest`-shaped payload for a one-field change. It recomputes the SLA due-date targets against the new priority immediately, so an escalated ticket's own deadlines update in the same action rather than waiting for an unrelated future edit.
- **`ticket_escalations` snapshots `previous_priority`/`new_priority`/`escalated_to_admin_id` at the moment of escalation**, and its FK to the rule is `nullOnDelete` — the historical fact of what happened survives a rule being edited or deleted afterward, the same "audit link cleared, historical snapshot preserved" pattern SLA Management's own `sla_policy_id` retrofit established for tickets. Verified directly: deleting the governing rule left the escalation record's priority snapshot and admin link fully intact, only the rule reference itself went null.
- **No manual create/edit UI for `ticket_escalations`** — these rows are exclusively system-generated by the "Escalate" action, so a hand-entry form would let an admin fabricate history that never happened. Exposed instead as a plain **read-only** report screen (`TicketEscalationController@index`, no create/edit/destroy at all), the same "controller only, index-only" shape every read-only report in this project uses (e.g. Employee Asset Tracking) — plus a compact escalation-history block inline on each ticket's own edit view.

Scope decision
