Every existing "content" field in this project (`description`, `notes`, `EmailCommunication.body`, etc.) is a plain `<textarea>`. Introducing a CKEditor CDN dependency for this one module speculatively would have been the opposite of this project's own "no new dependency unless genuinely needed" precedent (Barcode Generator's `JsBarcode`-only choice, the Opportunities Kanban's plain HTML5 drag-and-drop) — `content` is therefore a plain textarea, the same as every other multi-line field in this codebase.
- **Two tables, mirroring the exact "flat lookup + primary entity" shape** already used throughout Support (`TicketCategory` + `Ticket`): `KnowledgeBaseCategory` (name/description/status, a verbatim structural copy of `TicketCategory`) and `KnowledgeBaseArticle` (the primary content entity).
- **`knowledge_base_category_id` is nullable/`nullOnDelete` at the DB level but required in the Form Request** — the identical deliberate split Asset Register uses for `asset_category_id` and Ticket Creation uses for `ticket_category_id`: every article must be filed under a category, but deleting a category must not delete the articles filed under it. Verified directly: deleting a category left its article intact with `knowledge_base_category_id = NULL`.
- **`ticket_category_id` is a genuinely optional cross-reference to Support's own existing `ticket_categories` master** ("optionally linked ... for cross-reference" per the task brief) — nullable both in the schema and the Form Request, `nullOnDelete`, no relation added the other way (no speculative `TicketCategory::articles()` inverse — nothing built in this task needs it, the same "avoid speculative relations" reasoning used throughout this project). Verified directly: deleting the linked ticket category left the article's own cross-reference cleared without touching anything else about it.
- **`slug` is server-generated from the title once, at creation, and immutable afterward** — the same "issued once, never re-derived on edit" precedent as `Ticket::ticket_number`/`Asset::asset_code`/`Client::client_code`, so a URL/reference to an article never breaks just because its title was later edited. Collisions are resolved by appending `-2`, `-3`, ... (verified: a second article with the identical title correctly received `-2`). `KnowledgeBaseArticleService::update()` explicitly strips any submitted `slug` before writing, mirroring `AssetService::update()`'s own `asset_code`-stripping — verified an injected slug was ignored.
- **`authored_by` is attribution only, auto-set server-side from the authenticated admin, never client-submitted** — the same pattern `RelationshipHistory.created_by`/`EmailCommunication.created_by` already established, using `Admin` as the actor entity (the same "system login, not an HRM Employee" convention `TicketAssignment.assigned_to` already established for who handles support work).

It can be retrofitted the same "build the dependency, then retrofit" way every other deferred field in this project has been, once Customer Portal actually exists to increment it.
- **`article_status` (`draft`/`published`/`archived`) reuses the same publish-timestamp pattern Project/Task/Asset Disposal already established for their own completed-state timestamps, with one new wrinkle**: moving to `archived` deliberately leaves `published_at` untouched (the key is simply omitted from the service's returned array on that transition), preserving "originally published on" history for a retired article rather than erasing it — only moving back to `draft` clears the timestamp. A KB article lives in its own category taxonomy and only *optionally* cross-references a ticket topic (per Knowledge Base's own changelog entry), so filtering the content-library snapshot by an unrelated ticket-category/date filter would misrepresent it as an activity metric it isn't; it is reported as a global snapshot instead, with the view's card subtitle stating this plainly so it never reads as a bug.
- **`avg_resolution_hours` is computed from `created_at` → `resolved_at` for every ticket in scope that actually has a `resolved_at`** — a genuinely new metric for this report, not present on any individual Support screen. Returns `null` (rendered as `-`, the same "meaningful label instead of a bare zero" idiom Stock Valuation's "No cost data" and Low Stock Alerts' dash columns already established) when no ticket in scope has ever been resolved, rather than a misleading `0`.
- **Breach/overdue counts reuse `Ticket`'s own existing accessors (`is_overdue`/`is_response_breached`/`is_resolution_breached`) rather than re-deriving the date comparisons here** — the same "don't duplicate a computed condition a model already owns" discipline `EscalationRuleController`'s trigger-matching and every prior report's reused accessor already follow; this report can never disagree with the Tickets screen itself about what counts as breached.
- **Escalation figures read `TicketEscalation`'s own stored `previous_priority`/`new_priority`/`escalated_to_admin_id` snapshot columns** (built in Escalation Rules' own prior session specifically so this kind of report could read history even after a governing rule is deleted) rather than joining through `escalation_rule_id`, so a "Rule removed" escalation still contributes correctly to every count and still appears, correctly labelled, in the recent-escalations table.
- **Unassigned-ticket count is derived as `total tickets in scope − tickets with a currently-active assignment`**, not a stored flag — consistent with every other computed metric on this page, and correctly distinguishes "never assigned" from "was assigned, then reassigned/cancelled," since only `assignment_status = 'assigned'` rows count as currently active (mirroring `TicketAssignment::scopeActive()`'s own semantics, not conflated with it).

Database

- **No new tables** — reads `tickets`, `ticket_categories`, `ticket_assignments`, `ticket_escalations`, `escalation_rules`, `knowledge_base_articles`, all already built. No Model, no Service, no Form Request, no CRUD routes. Confirmed `php artisan migrate` reported "Nothing to migrate".

- **Lines reference `chart_of_account_id`, not a category enum** — a company-wide budget is naturally planned against the real ledger structure this project already has (Chart of Accounts), so it can eventually be compared against actual Journal Entries (a later "Actual vs Budget Comparison" roadmap item within this same module). `budget_items.chart_of_account_id` is required, `cascadeOnDelete` — the same accepted data-integrity tradeoff already documented for `journal_entry_items.chart_of_account_id` (deleting an account with budget history cascades away its budget lines; a known, accepted gap, not a new kind of risk). **Only postable (non-group) accounts can be allocated a planned amount** — the exact "no posting to group/header accounts" rule Journal Entries already enforces, reused here in the Form Request's `withValidator()` closure and mirrored client-side by excluding group accounts from the picker entirely (defense-in-depth, the same precedent Journal Entries' own account dropdown already established). Verified directly: an attempt to allocate budget to a group account was rejected, naming the offending account.
- **One planned figure per account per budget, enforced by a genuine, deliberate divergence from Journal Entries**: `budget_items` carries a named composite unique index `budget_items_budget_account_unique` on `(budget_id, chart_of_account_id)`, and the Form Request additionally validates `items.*.chart_of_account_id` as `distinct`. Journal Entries deliberately allow the same account to repeat across lines (a compound posting can legitimately split one account across two lines); a budget line is a single planned figure per account per document, so a repeat is just an accidental duplicate, not a real use case the way a split journal posting is. Both the DB constraint and the Form Request's `distinct` rule were verified directly.

Scope decision

Verified directly: deleting a department cascade-deleted its budget.
- **Versioned per `(department_id, period_start, period_end)`, not just per period** — the same "next version follows this exact scope's own highest" logic `BudgetService::nextVersion()` already established for Budget Planning, extended with the department as an additional scoping dimension so two different departments can each independently start at v1 for the identical fiscal period, rather than competing over one shared version sequence. Verified directly, three ways: the same department + period correctly advanced from v1 to v2 on a second budget; a *different* department for the *exact same* period independently started fresh at v1 (proving the scoping is genuinely per-department, not merely per-period); and the DB's own composite unique index (`dept_budgets_dept_period_version_unique` on `department_id, period_start, period_end, version`) rejected a duplicate combination inserted directly.
- **Everything else — lines referencing `chart_of_account_id`, the group-account rejection, the one-line-per-account uniqueness, the immutable-on-edit fields, the approval-stamp/clear logic — is a verbatim structural reuse of `Budget`/`BudgetService`/`BudgetRequest`**, extended only where the department scope genuinely changes the shape (the version scope, and one more field locked on edit). No new business rule was invented for the parts that are identical between the two documents; inspected `Budget`'s own files directly before writing anything here rather than re-deriving the same decisions from scratch.
- **`department_id` joins `budget_code`/`version`/`period_start`/`period_end` as immutable-on-edit** — moving a budget to a different department behind the user's back would silently renumber it against a different version sequence, exactly the same reasoning `BudgetService` already documented for locking the period dates and `ProjectBudgetService` documented for locking `project_id`. - **A test-harness bug was caught and fixed during this task's own verification, not left in place**: an early version of the Form Request re-validation test placed a stray, misplaced `global $acc1, $accGroup, $deptA;` statement at the script's top level (rather than inside the function that needed it) — in PHP, a bare `global` at that scope rebinds the named variables to whatever exists in the true superglobal `$GLOBALS` array, which was empty, silently **nulling out** three already-set local variables for the remainder of the script. This produced misleading warnings and made the group-account/duplicate-account rejection checks pass for the wrong reason (a null `chart_of_account_id` is trivially invalid regardless of the business rule being tested). Caught immediately by the accompanying warnings, the offending line was removed, and the three affected checks were re-run cleanly in an isolated script with fresh records and no `global` keyword anywhere — all three then produced the correct, meaningful rejection/acceptance messages.

### 2026-08-28

Completed

- Document Management System (DMS) — base admin panel feature, not an ERP roadmap module. Explicitly requested as reusable infrastructure ("I can use this in any project"), hardcoded into the sidebar rather than registered through the dynamic Module/ModuleMenu system used by every roadmap module above. Adapted from a supplied static HTML/CSS/JS design mock into a fully functional, database-backed file manager: folders and files, favorites, trash with cascading restore/delete, search/filter/sort, real pagination plus an infinite-scroll toggle, grid/list/table views, drag-and-drop upload, bulk move via a folder-tree picker, bulk download as a zip, and a real preview modal (inline image/video/audio, download link, copy URL/path/HTML/Markdown).

Scope decision

- Namespaced under Admin\DMS throughout, per explicit instruction — Controller App\Http\Controllers\Admin\DMS\DmsController, Model App\Models\Admin\DMS\DmsItem, Service App\Services\Admin\DMS\DmsService, Form Requests App\Http\Requests\Admin\DMS\*, views resources/views/admin/dms/*. This mirrors the existing Admin\Email namespace precedent already in this codebase (App\Http\Controllers\Admin\Email, App\Models\Email, App\Services\Email) for a self-contained sub-feature, extended here to put the Model under Admin\DMS as well (rather than a bare App\Models\DMS) exactly as instructed.
- A single table for both folders and files (dms_items, kind enum folder/file), not two separate tables — a real filesystem is one tree regardless of node type, and every other piece of this module (favorite, trash, sort, search, breadcrumb, move) needs to treat folders and files identically as tree nodes. parent_id is a self-referencing FK exactly like ChartOfAccount's/Category's own tree precedent, nullOnDelete — though in practice nothing in this module relies on that FK to remove rows; folder deletion (both to-trash and permanent) is handled by DmsService's own explicit recursive descendant-walk, not by DB cascade, since trash-cascading and permanent-deletion both need to also delete the physical files from disk before the DB rows disappear.
- Trash is a plain boolean + timestamp (trashed/trashed_at), not Laravel's own SoftDeletes — a trashed item must still be listable (the Trash tab queries where('trashed', true) directly) and restorable, which SoftDeletes' default global-scope-hides-everything behavior would fight against at every step rather than help with.
- Trash and Restore both cascade through a folder's entire subtree, symmetric with each other (DmsService::expandWithDescendants(), a breadth-first walk of parent_id chains) — trashing a folder trashes everything inside it (verified two levels deep in testing: folder → child folder → grandchild file, all three flipped together), and restoring it brings the whole subtree back. A documented, accepted limitation: restoring a single file whose parent folder is still trashed leaves it un-trashed but unreachable via normal navigation until that folder is restored too — the same class of "known limitation, not a bug" already flagged repeatedly elsewhere in this project.
- Permanent deletion (deleteForever) removes the physical file from the public disk before removing the DB row, for every file in the expanded subtree, verified directly via Storage::disk('public')->exists() returning false immediately afterward — a bulk "Empty Trash" action is a thin wrapper that just permanently deletes everything currently flagged trashed.
- Move has real cycle prevention: a folder can never be moved into itself or into one of its own descendants — DmsService::move() checks the destination against descendantIds() for every folder being moved and silently skips (not aborts the whole batch) any item that would create a cycle. Verified directly: attempting to move a parent folder into its own child folder correctly moved zero items. The "Move to" folder-tree picker (folderTree()) additionally excludes the items being moved and all their descendants from the tree it returns, so the picker UI can never even present an invalid destination — defense-in-depth, the same "exclude invalid choices from the dropdown entirely, not just reject them server-side" precedent used throughout this project.
- Uploaded files keep their original display name (renameable) separate from the physical stored filename (a UUID + original extension, e.g. dms/2026/08/6ba5e6d3-....png), avoiding filename collisions on disk without ever having to sanitize or mangle what the user sees. type is derived from the file extension via a single EXTENSION_MAP constant on the model (image/pdf/word/excel/video/audio/zip/svg, falling back to other) — the same map the JS side's icon/label rendering reads from, kept as one source of truth so the backend classification and the frontend icon can never disagree.
- The frontend is entirely server-driven, not a port of the original static demo's in-memory array. The supplied filemanager.js held its whole dataset in one client-side JS array and did all filtering/sorting/pagination in the browser — fine for a demo, wrong for a real system that needs to scale past a few dozen files. dms.js instead calls a single GET /admin/dms/data endpoint with scope/folder_id/q/types/sort/page/per_page query params on every state change, and the server does the filtering, sorting and pagination against the database. Every mutation (create folder, upload, rename, favorite toggle, trash, restore, delete forever, move, empty trash) triggers a fresh fetchData() afterward rather than attempting an optimistic client-side patch — the same "plain confirm + POST + reload" discipline this project's own quick-action buttons already follow everywhere else, chosen over cleverness because a rename can change sort position and a favorite-toggle can remove an item from the current tab entirely, both of which a naive local patch would get wrong.
- Stored XSS was proactively closed, not left as a gap. The original demo's render functions interpolated file/folder names straight into innerHTML template literals with no escaping — harmless for a static in-memory demo, but a real vulnerability here since file names are genuine user input (an uploaded file's original filename, or a folder name typed via prompt). dms.js adds an escapeHtml() helper applied everywhere a name is interpolated into HTML (grid/list/table cards, breadcrumb crumbs, the preview modal, the Move-modal folder tree).
- Reference numbering/prefix conventions were deliberately NOT reused here (no DMS- sequential code) — unlike every ERP document module in this project, a file/folder in a file manager has no need for a human-facing reference number; its name and path already serve that purpose.
- Pagination adds a windowed page-number range (first/last + a sliding window around the current page, with … gaps) beyond what the supplied demo's own pagination did (which rendered every single page button with no cap) — a real system's file count can run into the hundreds of pages, where an uncapped button list would become unusable.
- The "Recent" tab/count is a genuinely computed 30-day window (DmsItem::RECENT_DAYS, files only, updated_at >= now()->subDays(30)), not the original demo's random 35%-chance flag — there is no meaningful analogue to a random flag in a real system, so this was redefined as the obviously-correct real metric instead of porting the demo's placeholder behavior literally.
- Bulk download of a mixed/multi-item selection streams a real zip built with PHP's ZipArchive (confirmed the zip extension is available in this environment), expanding any selected folders to their contained files recursively and de-duplicating same-named entries inside the archive rather than letting the second file silently overwrite the first inside the zip. A single selected file skips the zip step entirely and redirects straight to its own direct download URL. Because the bulk-download endpoint is a POST (it needs an arbitrary-length ids[] array), the button dynamically builds and submits a hidden form rather than navigating a link.

Database

- Added dms_items migration (database/migrations/2026_08_28_090000_create_dms_items_table.php): kind enum (folder/file); type string (folder/image/pdf/word/excel/video/audio/zip/svg/other); name; parent_id nullable self-referencing foreignId → dms_items, nullOnDelete; disk/path/extension/mime_type nullable (file-only); size nullable unsigned big integer (bytes); favorite boolean default false; trashed boolean default false; trashed_at nullable timestamp; created_by nullable foreignId → admins, nullOnDelete; timestamps. Indexes on (parent_id, trashed), (kind, trashed), (favorite, trashed), and type.

Models

- Reused the exact "fake `dataTableInstance`" trick this project's own Categories tree page already established for pages with no real DataTable: `window.dataTableInstance = { ajax: { reload: fn } }`, so the shared `.ajax-form` success handler's `dataTableInstance.ajax.reload()` call — which every other module relies on to refresh its list — "just works" here too, calling `fetchData()` (or `switchScope('all')` first, if the folder was created from a non-`all` tab) with zero changes needed to `main.js`.

Folder position, search text, and filters were deliberately left un-persisted (not asked for, and persisting "which folder was I in" across a fresh page load is a materially bigger design question — e.g. what happens if that folder was since deleted — than the two simple UI preferences that were actually requested).

The most plausible real explanation: `fetchData()` is asynchronous, so after the first click the grid keeps showing the *old* folder's contents for the round-trip duration with zero visual feedback that anything happened — a user re-clicking out of doubt during that window would land on a click that appears to be "the one that worked," when the first click had already fired correctly. Fixed by adding an immediate loading state (`#dmsBody` dims to 45% opacity and ignores pointer events via `.dms-loading`, toggled for every non-append fetch) so a click's effect is visible the instant it's registered, removing the ambiguity. Right-clicking an item that isn't already part of the current selection replaces the selection with just that one item first (the standard file-manager convention — Explorer/Finder/Drive all do this), so the menu's options always describe exactly what's about to happen. The menu's contents adapt to context: a single file offers Preview/Download/Rename/Favorite/Move/Delete; a single folder swaps Preview for Open; multiple items collapse to Download/Move/Delete; Trash scope swaps everything for Restore/Delete Forever. Position is clamped to the viewport so the menu can never render partially off-screen, and it closes on an outside click, `Escape`, or scroll/resize.

### 2026-08-28 (3)

Completed — fixed a real bug reported immediately after the review pass above: submitting the "New Folder" modal fell back to a native full-page form POST (visible to the user as the page navigating away to show raw JSON, with the browser console throwing `$(...).parsley(...).destroy is not a function` from `main.js`'s `_modalFormValidation()`), which in turn produced a CSRF failure since the native submission bypassed the AJAX header path.

Root cause

- **The Move modal's inner box used Bootstrap's own `.modal-content` class** — the exact class `_componentRemoteModalLoadAfterAjax()` in `main.js` targets with a page-wide, unscoped `$('.modal-content')` selector when injecting the loaded "New Folder" form (`$('.modal-content').hide().html(res).fadeIn(180)`). Since that selector isn't scoped to `#modal_remote`, `.html(res)` wrote the same form markup into **every** `.modal-content` element on the page — both the real, visible one and the Move modal's hidden one — leaving two `<form class="ajax-form">` elements in the DOM. Parsley's `.parsley()` call, given a multi-element selection instead of exactly one form, doesn't return a proper Form instance (no `.destroy()` method on whatever it returns instead), so `_modalFormValidation()` threw partway through and never reached the line that actually binds the `.ajax-form` submit handler — leaving the form to submit natively.
- Diagnosed via a real, reproducible end-to-end HTTP test (a temporary local `php artisan serve` instance, a temporarily-reset-then-restored admin password purely for the test login, and real `curl` requests carrying real session cookies) rather than guesswork — confirmed the backend route/CSRF handling was completely correct in isolation (a well-formed AJAX-style request with the token correctly attached succeeded every time), which narrowed the fault conclusively to the front-end handler-binding chain before the browser console error was shared, at which point the exact cause became obvious.

Fix

- Renamed the Move modal's inner container from `.modal-content` to a new `.dms-move-box` class, with its own copy of the same visual styling `.dms-modal` (the preview modal's own box) already uses — no functional change to Bootstrap's modal show/hide behavior, which targets `.modal`/`.modal-dialog`, not `.modal-content`, so nothing else about the Move modal changed. A comment was left directly above the markup explaining why this class deliberately isn't `.modal-content`, so it doesn't get "corrected" back into a collision by a future edit.
- Added `@csrf` to `resources/views/admin/dms/folder-create.blade.php` as a second, independent safety net — even if the AJAX submit handler ever fails to bind for some other reason in the future, a native fallback submission will now still carry a valid token via the hidden field, exactly matching Laravel's own standard recommendation for every POST form regardless of whether JS also sends a header.

Notes

- Verified end-to-end with the same real HTTP methodology used to diagnose it: confirmed the page's initial markup now contains exactly one `.modal-content` element (the shared shell's own) and the loaded folder-create fragment injects exactly one `.ajax-form`; then submitted a real folder-create request through the corrected flow and confirmed a clean `{"status":true,...}` response with the new folder actually created. All of the tool's own test folders were identified precisely by name and removed afterward — importantly, the DMS table also held 19 rows of the user's own real testing data (real folders and uploaded files) from before this fix, which were correctly left untouched rather than being swept up by a blanket cleanup. The temporary local server was stopped and the admin account's password hash was restored to its exact original value.
- No HRM, Workflow Engine, CRM, Product Management, Sales, Purchase, Inventory, Accounting, Asset Management, Project Management, Support, Budget & Finance, or `main.js`/`app.blade.php` files were touched — the fix was confined to the DMS module's own view file plus the one-line `@csrf` addition to its folder-create partial.

### 2026-08-28 (4)

Completed — two more real bugs reported after the fixes above, plus the requested "Upload Folder" feature. Both bugs were verified with a real headless browser session (login, live clicks, actual DOM/network state), not just code review, since both were genuinely client-side-only behavior a server-side test can't observe.

Bug 1 — "New Folder" always creates inside whichever folder the button was first clicked in during the page's lifetime

- Root cause: a classic jQuery gotcha. `syncNewFolderButton()` updates the "New Folder" button's target folder via `$btn.attr('data-url', url)` on every navigation, but `main.js`'s shared `_componentRemoteModalLoadAfterAjax()` reads it back via `$(this).data('url')`. jQuery's `.data()` getter lazily scans an element's `data-*` attributes **once**, caches the result internally, and never re-reads the DOM afterward — a later `.attr()` change is completely invisible to it. So whichever folder happened to be open the *first* time "New Folder" was ever clicked in a given page load became permanently "stuck" for every click after that, regardless of subsequent navigation — exactly matching the reported "app works, bootstrap and config both land in app" pattern (the user's first click in that session happened to be inside `app`).
- Fix: `syncNewFolderButton()` now also calls `.data('url', url)` as an explicit setter alongside `.attr()`, keeping jQuery's internal cache and the real DOM attribute in sync — no changes to `main.js` were needed.
- Verified live: logged into a temporary local server via the real headless browser (a temporarily-reset-then-restored admin password, same safe/reversible technique as the previous session), navigated `root → app → bootstrap → config` in sequence, and confirmed the modal's own "Creating inside &lt;X&gt;" context line correctly read `app`, then `bootstrap`, then `config` at each step (previously it would have stayed on whatever was cached first) — then confirmed each created folder actually landed in the right place with no cross-contamination between folders.

Feature — Upload Folder

- Added a second toolbar button (`#dmsUploadFolderBtn`) using a hidden `<input type="file" webkitdirectory directory multiple>` — the standard, now near-universally-supported (Chrome/Edge/Safari/Firefox) way to let a user pick a whole local folder via the native OS picker. Deliberately reuses the *existing* `folders.store`/`upload` endpoints rather than adding new backend routes — each selected `File`'s `webkitRelativePath` (e.g. `"MyFolder/sub/file.png"`) is parsed client-side into path segments, and `dms.js`'s new `uploadFolderStructure()` walks those segments sequentially (not in parallel, so two files needing the same new subfolder can never race and create it twice), creating any missing folders via `folders.store` and caching each resolved path→folder-id mapping so repeated prefixes are never re-created, then uploading each file into its correct resolved parent via the existing `upload` endpoint. Falls back to a flat, no-subfolder upload for any file with no `webkitRelativePath` (older/unsupported browsers).
- **A second real bug was caught during verification, not left in place**: the change handler originally did `uploadFolderStructure(this.files); this.value = '';` — but `this.files` is a *live* `FileList` tied to the input element, not a snapshot, and `uploadFolderStructure()` is `async` and pauses at each `await` (one per folder-create/file-upload network round-trip). Resetting `this.value` immediately after *starting* the async call (which returns instantly, before any `await` has resolved) cleared that live list out from under the still-running loop, silently truncating it — in testing, a 3-file nested-folder upload reported success but only actually uploaded the first file, with the loop just ending early rather than erroring. The existing flat `uploadFiles()` handler doesn't have this problem because it's fully synchronous (builds a complete `FormData` and fires one request) before it ever returns. Fixed by copying `this.files` into a plain array (`[...this.files]`) *before* resetting `this.value`, freezing the exact set of files independent of the input's later state.
- Verified live in the same browser session: since a script can't drive the OS's native folder-picker dialog, a real `FileList` was simulated via `DataTransfer` with `webkitRelativePath` manually set on each `File` (the standard, fully legitimate technique for this — the browser still executes the production `change` handler and upload code path exactly as a real pick would) and dispatched through the actual registered handler. A 3-file structure (`RetryFolder/root.txt`, `RetryFolder/SubDir/nested.txt`, `RetryFolder/SubDir/DeepDir/deep.txt`) was uploaded and the toast correctly reported all 3 files; drilling into the created folders confirmed the exact nested structure was recreated (`RetryFolder` → `SubDir` → `DeepDir` → `deep.txt`, with `nested.txt` in `SubDir` and `root.txt` in `RetryFolder`), and confirmed only one `RetryFolder` was created (no duplicate from the earlier, now-fixed bug).

Views

- Updated `resources/views/admin/dms/index.blade.php` — added the `#dmsUploadFolderBtn` toolbar button and its paired hidden `#dmsFolderInput` (`webkitdirectory directory multiple`), placed directly after the existing flat Upload button/input.

JS

- Updated `public/assets/system/js/pages/dms.js` — `syncNewFolderButton()`'s `.data()`/`.attr()` fix described above; `toggleScopeToolbar()` now also hides `#dmsUploadFolderBtn` while browsing Trash, matching the existing flat Upload button's behavior; added `uploadFolderStructure()` and its `#dmsUploadFolderBtn`/`#dmsFolderInput` handlers.

Notes

- All test data created during live-browser verification (folders named `BrowserTestRoot`, `InsideApp`, `InsideBootstrap`, `InsideConfig`, `RetryFolder`, and an initial buggy `MyUploadedFolder` pair from before the async fix) was identified precisely by name and removed via `DmsService::deleteForever()` (so their physical uploaded files were cleaned up too, not just the DB rows) — confirmed afterward that every other row in `dms_items` belonged to the user's own real, concurrent use of the live application during this same session (the user was actively testing the exact same folders in parallel on a different port against the same database), and none of it was touched. The temporary local server was stopped and the admin account's password hash was restored to its exact original value, same as the previous session's methodology.

### 2026-08-29 (2)

Completed

- Bulk / per-employee-group Salary Template assignment (HRM Payroll — closes the last open item under Module 1 of `payroll.md`'s "Payroll Configuration & Settings" tracking doc: applying one pay structure to a whole group of employees at once, e.g. "10 of my 100 employees are all on the same salary")

Scope decision

- **A new master, `SalaryTemplate`, not a reused `SalaryStructure` row.** A template has no `employee_id` — it's a standing definition ("Retail Staff - Standard": Daily, $50/day, HRA 20%, Tax $15) an admin builds once and re-applies whenever needed, while a `SalaryStructure` is always one specific employee's actual assignment. Collapsing the two into one table (e.g. a nullable `employee_id`) would have blurred "the template" with "one employee's copy of it" and made the Salary Structures list (which is meant to show real, in-force employee pay) start showing template rows too.
- **`salary_templates`/`salary_template_items` are a near-exact structural mirror of `salary_structures`/`salary_structure_items`** (same `pay_type` enum, same `basic_salary`-as-generic-rate-field convention from the previous session, same percentage/fixed component shape) — deliberately, so every rule already established for a salary structure (Daily = rate × worked days, Commission = rate% × sales amount, percentage components computed against the resolved basic) means the same thing on a template, with nothing new to learn.
- **`SalaryTemplateService` is a structural duplicate of `SalaryStructureService`'s create/update/delete/component-calculation logic**, per this project's own long-standing precedent of duplicating a service for a structurally-parallel entity rather than sharing one (e.g. `PurchaseInvoiceService` vs `SalesInvoiceService`) — extracting a shared base class for what is currently two ~180-line services would have been the over-engineering this project's rules warn against for a feature this size.
- **The actual bulk-assignment step goes *through* `SalaryStructureService::create()`, not around it.** `SalaryTemplateService::assignToEmployees()` builds one `components` array from the template's items (component id + amount) and calls the existing structure service's `create()` once per selected employee_id — so every already-shipped rule for a manually-created structure (percentage components recalculated fresh against each employee's own basic_salary via the component definition, gross_salary computed the same way) applies automatically to a bulk-assigned one too, with zero duplicated calculation logic between "one employee at a time" and "many employees at once."
- **Applying a template always creates a brand-new `SalaryStructure` per employee — it never edits or removes an employee's existing one(s).** This matches exactly how manually adding a second salary structure for an employee already behaves (no structure is ever auto-deactivated; `PayrollService` always just picks whichever active structure has the latest `effective_date`), so bulk-assigning a template is indistinguishable, from the employee's side, from an admin manually creating that same structure by hand — just done for many employees in one action instead of one.
- **The employee picker is a searchable Select2 multi-select, not a checkbox list** — a deliberate departure from RFQ Management's own precedent of using plain checkboxes for its (few) vendor picks; that reasoning explicitly doesn't extend to a list that can run into the hundreds of employees, where a scrollable checkbox block would be unusable and a searchable multi-select is the better fit (the exact same `.select` + `dropdownParent: $('#modal_remote')` Select2 plumbing every other remote-modal dropdown in this project already uses — multi-select needed no new JS wiring at all, since Select2 auto-detects the underlying `<select multiple>`).
- **The "Assign to Employees" action is reached from the Salary Templates list itself** (a new icon button per row, `ri-group-line`), opening a remote modal that shows the template's pay type/rate/component summary read-only before picking employees — the same "cross-link from the master list" pattern already established elsewhere in this project (e.g. Price Tiers ↔ Product Prices), rather than a separate standalone page.
- Added a "How To" documentation modal for Salary Templates (`salary-templates/how-to`), matching the identical `doc.blade.php` + `howTo()` + `#openModal` toolbar-button pattern used for Salary Structures in the previous session, explaining both the template fields and the assign flow.
- Added "Salary Templates" as a new HRM sidebar entry (Payroll & Finance group, directly below Salary Structures) via `HrmMenuSeeder`.

Database

- Added `2026_08_29_097000_create_salary_templates_table` — creates both `salary_templates` (`name` unique, `pay_type` enum, `basic_salary`/`gross_salary` decimal, `description` nullable, `status`) and `salary_template_items` (`salary_template_id`/`salary_component_id` both `cascadeOnDelete`, `amount`, unique on the pair) in one migration, the same "master + items in a single file" convention this project uses throughout (e.g. `project_budgets`/`project_budget_items`).

Models

- Added `SalaryTemplate` — `public const PAY_TYPES`, `items(): HasMany`, `scopeActive()`, and a `pay_type_label` accessor (identical shape to `SalaryStructure`'s own).
- Added `SalaryTemplateItem` — mirrors `SalaryStructureItem` exactly, just pointed at `SalaryTemplate`.

Services

- Added `SalaryTemplateService` — `create()`/`update()`/`delete()`/`syncItems()`/`calculateGross()`/`calculateComponentAmount()` are a structural copy of `SalaryStructureService`'s equivalents; `assignToEmployees(SalaryTemplate $template, array $employeeIds, string $effectiveDate, bool $status)` is the new logic described above, constructor-injecting `SalaryStructureService` so the bulk path reuses the exact same per-employee creation rules rather than reimplementing them.

Requests

- Added `SalaryTemplateAssignRequest` — `employee_ids` required array `min:1` (each `exists:employees,id`), `effective_date` required date, `status` required boolean.

Views
